hints.quote: Know the 4 common globular protein motifs
hints.take: Most globular proteins are all α, all β, α/β (helices and strands intermingled) or α+β (separate α-helical and β-sheet domains).

hints.quote: Understand how protein structures are stabilized and why some portions of proteins are marginally stable
hints.take: A fold is stabilized by many intramolecular hydrogen bonds and by burying hydrophobic side chains away from water; it is only marginally stable, so parts flex, which binding, catalysis and shape changes need.

hints.quote: Stability: reduction of surface to volume ratio. Genetic economy and efficiency. Bringing catalytic sites together. Cooperativity
hints.take: Quaternary structure's four advantages: stability (less surface facing water), genetic economy and efficiency (small subunits made accurately), catalytic sites formed between subunits, and cooperativity.

hints.quote: Do not memorize charts
hints.take: Skip the electronegativity cutoff numbers; know that a growing electronegativity difference moves a bond from nonpolar covalent to polar covalent to ionic.

hints.quote: Do not memorize
hints.take: Skip how much of the body is water and how much we drink a day; know water's properties and why they come from its hydrogen bonds.

hints.quote: You will probably discuss other buffers in other organ module courses, but we'll just focus on the example of the bicarbonate buffer system
hints.take: For this lecture, know the bicarbonate buffer: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, with carbonic anhydrase in red cells speeding the first step.

hints.quote: Don't memorize structures, but know that A &G are purines, C, T, U are pyrimidines
hints.take: Skip the bases' ring structures; know adenine and guanine are purines and cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines.

hints.quote: do not memorize
hints.take: Skip the chart of lipid structures; know that lipids are defined by their low solubility in water, and the main kinds: triglycerides, phospholipids and steroids.

hints.quote: BUT….ultimately sufficient hyperkalemia locks the Na+ channels in the inactive state.
hints.take: A mild rise in K+ brings the membrane closer to threshold, but enough hyperkalemia depolarizes it so far that the Na+ channels stay inactivated: nerve and muscle can't fire, so muscles go weak. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes and also lowers excitability.

hints.quote: A 10-fold concentration gradient of a monovalent ion is equivalent, as a driving force, to an electrical potential of 60 mV.
hints.take: E = (60/z) log([out]/[in]) at 37 °C: 100 mM K+ inside and 10 mM outside gives −60 mV; an anion flips the sign; Ca2+ uses z = 2.

hints.quote: The electrogenic Na-pump (3Na, 2K) sets up the ionic gradient but only contributes little to membrane potential.
hints.take: The resting potential comes from the K+ leak (K+ conductance far above Na+, so it sits near E(K+)); the pump builds the gradients and adds only a few millivolts directly.

hints.quote: REMEMBER ‘g’ Salts dissociate e.g. NaCl = 2, MgCl2 = 3 Non-electrolytes e.g. Glucose = 1
hints.take: Osmotic pressure counts particles: multiply the concentration by g (NaCl 2, MgCl2 3, glucose 1) and by the reflection coefficient (0 = crosses freely, draws no water; 1 = impermeant, full effect).

hints.quote: NOTE: ALWAYS activate a G protein, slower response time
hints.take: Ionotropic receptors are ion channels and act fast; metabotropic receptors always work through a G protein and second messengers (cAMP, Ca2+, IP3), so they are slower.

hints.quote: NOTE: SODIUM IS A KEY PLAYER!
hints.take: Secondary active transport runs on the Na+ gradient the Na+/K+ pump makes: cotransport moves the solute with Na+ (SGLT1, Na+–K+–2Cl−), countertransport against it (Na+/Ca2+, Na+/H+).

hints.quote: FOR REFERENCE ONLY! DO NOT MEMORIZE!
hints.take: Skip the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation. Know that when a membrane is permeable to several ions, each counts by its relative permeability, so the resting potential sits nearest E(K+); work single-ion equilibrium potentials with the Nernst equation.

hints.quote: * Do not need to memorize neuropeptide list*
hints.take: Skip which neuropeptides go with which small-molecule transmitter. Know the classes: amino acids (glutamate, GABA, glycine), biogenic amines, purines and acetylcholine are made in the terminal; neuropeptides (3–36 amino acids, such as substance P and enkephalin) are made in the cell body.

hints.quote: *Do not memorize – just examples of differences
hints.take: Skip the receptor-family figure. Know that only cells with the matching receptor respond, and that a signal is relayed by phosphorylation and second messengers (cAMP, Ca2+), often to transcription factors that change which proteins the cell makes.

hints.quote: Just examples of cell rates, not tested on individual rates
hints.take: Skip how many hours each cell type takes to divide. Know the point: some cancers divide more slowly than some normal cells, and a tumor outgrows its tissue because a larger share of its cells are dividing.

hints.quote: What are you supposed to know from the lecture: (for your exam)
hints.take: The definitions: an enzyme's catalytic power, specificity and regulation; coenzyme, cofactor, holoenzyme, apoenzyme and active site; how enzymes affect a reaction's thermodynamics; Km and Vmax; the turnover number (kcat) and catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km); single- versus double-displacement reactions; lock and key versus induced fit.

hints.quote: It is extremely important to appreciate this distinction
hints.take: ΔG, the overall free energy change, is related to the equilibrium constant (how far a reaction goes); ΔG‡, the free energy of activation, is related to the rate constant (how fast). Enzymes lower ΔG‡ only.

hints.quote: derive these equations
hints.take: Lineweaver-Burk is the reciprocal of Michaelis-Menten: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, so the y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the x-intercept −1/Km and the slope Km/Vmax.

hints.quote: What you need to know for your exam:
hints.take: What a thermodynamic system is (isolated, closed, open), the three laws, enthalpy and entropy, Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS), ATP's ionization states and its free energy of hydrolysis, and the kinds of biological work.

hints.quote: What to know: different types of steroid hormones, emphasized points of synthesis, examples, function and why they are important, mechanism of action
hints.take: The three types (glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex steroids) and what each does; synthesis from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex and gonads, starting in mitochondria, by P450 oxidations that need NADPH and O2; examples with their disorders (Cushing, Conn, Addison); and the mechanism: carrier proteins, then an intracellular receptor that changes transcription.

hints.quote: The point is that NADPH (the pentose shunt) & oxygen serve to remove electrons from cholesterol to make the first steroid in the pathway.
hints.take: Steroid synthesis is oxidative: mitochondrial P450 side-chain cleavage uses NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway and O2 to turn cholesterol into pregnenolone.

hints.quote: Do not memorize structures!
hints.take: Skip the steroid structures. Know that synthesis happens in the adrenal cortex (and gonads), that it is oxidation needing NADPH, that most of the enzymes are cytochrome P450s, and that their main job is to modify cholesterol's tail.

hints.quote: Do not memorize graphic
hints.take: Skip the metabolic map's details. Know the major pathways and what each one does: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, gluconeogenesis, the urea cycle, fatty acid β-oxidation and the pentose phosphate pathway.

hints.quote: C3 is the link between the different activation pathways and the functions of complement
hints.take: All three pathways (alternative, lectin, classical) build a C3 convertase, so cleaving C3 is the first step toward everything complement does: C3b opsonizes and helps build the C5 convertase that leads to the membrane attack complex, and C3a (with C5a) inflames.

hints.quote: The NF-kB signaling pathway is crucial for proinflammatory cytokine production.
hints.take: TLRs, NLRs and RLRs all turn on NF-κB, the transcription factor for the proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6); RLRs also turn on IRFs for type I interferon, and some NLRs form inflammasomes that activate IL-1β and IL-18.

hints.quote: Important integrin: LFA-1 (on neutrophils) and Mac-1 (on monocytes)
hints.take: Rolling is selectins binding mucin-like CAMs; tight binding is integrins binding Ig-superfamily CAMs, LFA-1 on neutrophils binding ICAM-1 in inflammation; CXCL8 (IL-8) draws the neutrophils in.

hints.quote: Resolution is equally important as activation in order to properly protect the host!
hints.take: Immune responses damage tissue as they clear a pathogen; acute inflammation that isn't resolved becomes chronic. Monocytes recruited late become M2 macrophages that help resolution and repair.

hints.quote: do not memorize figure, the point is that many CLRs bind pathogens with carbohydrate PAMPs and induce phagocytosis
hints.take: Skip the names of the individual C-type lectin receptors in the figure; know that CLRs bind carbohydrate PAMPs (fungi, mycobacteria, viruses, parasites) and trigger phagocytosis, and that mannose-binding lectin and the lung's surfactant proteins are soluble CLRs.

hints.quote: do not memorize chart, only know mediators that are highlighted as other examples of inflammatory mediators
hints.take: Skip the table of every mediator's source and actions; know the examples besides cytokines and chemokines: the lipids prostaglandins and leukotrienes, complement and histamine, which activate the endothelium, draw cells and contract smooth muscle.

hints.quote: do not memorize figure, know what PGs and LTs are and that they come from AA
hints.take: Skip the branches and products of the arachidonic acid pathway; know that prostaglandins and leukotrienes are potent proinflammatory lipid mediators made from arachidonic acid in membrane phospholipids, the link to the anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs block the cyclooxygenase step to prostaglandins).

hints.quote: For CD4+ T cells, know the details in this chart
hints.take: Know each helper subset's inducing cytokines, what it secretes and what it does: Th1 (IL-12; IFN-γ; activates macrophages and CD8 T cells), Th2 (IL-4; IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; IgE and eosinophils against parasites), Th17 (TGF-β, IL-6, IL-23; IL-17; neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi), Treg (IL-2, TGF-β, FoxP3; TGF-β and IL-10; tolerance) and Tfh (IL-21 and IL-6; germinal centers and antibody).

hints.quote: Know that the transcription factor Foxp3 is necessary for Treg differentiation and that TGFb and IL-10 are immunosuppressive/anti-inflammatory cytokines
hints.take: Tregs (CD4+, CD25+, FoxP3+) can't form without FoxP3; their TGF-β and IL-10 suppress self-reactive cells and calm inflammation.

hints.quote: IMPORTANT: Each B cell has one unique BCR (that recognizes an antigen epitope). The Abs produced by the B cell are identical to the BCR on the cell surface.
hints.take: One B cell, one specificity: the antibody a B cell and its plasma cells secrete binds the same epitope as its BCR. Class switching later changes the constant region, never the specificity.

hints.quote: do not memorize figure and poly-A or splice site info. Know that RNA splicing and not DNA recombination determines IgM versus IgD expression by a B cell
hints.take: Skip the polyadenylation and splice-site details; know that RNA splicing of one μ–δ transcript, not DNA recombination, lets a naive B cell show IgM and IgD together (and decides membrane-bound versus secreted antibody).

hints.quote: Components to know: Endosome/phagosome, Invariant chain, CLIP, HLA-DM
hints.take: MHC class II loading: engulfed protein is cut in an endosome or phagosome; the invariant chain blocks the groove on the way from the ER and is trimmed to CLIP; HLA-DM swaps CLIP for the peptide.

hints.quote: Don't need to know individually, but Tapasin, ERp57 and Calreticulin are proteins that stabilize MHC I and aid in peptide binding.
hints.take: For MHC class I loading, know the proteasome and TAP (peptides can't enter the ER without TAP); the ER helper proteins only as a group that steadies MHC I while it binds peptide.

hints.quote: *do not memorize, just FYI
hints.take: Said of the antibody drugs that block costimulatory molecules for cancer and of secukinumab, which blocks IL-17. Skip the drugs; know that B7–CD28 turns a naive T cell on and other costimulatory molecules turn it off later, and that Th17 cells' IL-17 calls in neutrophils and, unchecked, drives autoimmune inflammation.

hints.quote: *do not memorize figure
hints.take: Said of the NK cell receptor figure. Skip the individual receptor names; know that NK receptors are inhibitory (ITIM) or activating (ITAM), that many bind MHC I, and that an NK cell kills when activating signals win.

hints.quote: Impt note: IgG crosses the placenta, IgM does not
hints.take: In Rh disease the mother's first anti-RhD is IgM, which stays on her side; in a later Rh-positive pregnancy her memory B cells switch to IgG, which crosses the placenta and destroys fetal red cells. Anti-D (RhoGAM) prevents the first sensitization.

hints.quote: Important note: Unlike T cells, B cells go through germinal center processes throughout their “life span” which can slightly alter their BCRs. TCRs do not change once a thymocyte leaves the thymus
hints.take: A B cell's receptor can keep changing in germinal centers (class switching, somatic hypermutation); a T cell's receptor is fixed once it leaves the thymus.

hints.quote: This is a correlation NOT a cause
hints.take: An HLA allele raises the risk of an autoimmune disease by deciding which peptides are shown, but it doesn't cause it: about 90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis carry HLA-B27, and DR4 goes with rheumatoid arthritis.

hints.quote: Penicillin is notable. Can induce all 4 hypersensitivity reactions
hints.take: Its reactive bond binds host proteins and makes neoantigens: anaphylaxis (I), hemolytic anemia (II), serum sickness (III) and rashes (IV).

hints.quote: *do not memorize figure and poly-A or splice site info. Know that RNA splicing and not DNA recombination determines IgM versus IgD expression by a B cell
hints.take: Skip the poly-A and splice sites; know that one RNA transcript spliced two ways, not DNA recombination, lets a mature naive B cell carry IgM and IgD together.

hints.quote: Necrosis with preservation of architecture - coagulative necrosis
hints.take: Match each pattern to its setting: coagulative keeps the outlines (infarcts outside the brain); liquefactive in brain infarcts and infected tissue (pus); caseous in TB granulomas; fat necrosis from pancreatic lipases in acute pancreatitis; fibrinoid from immune complexes in vessel walls.

hints.quote: Cellular swelling - reversible injury
hints.take: Swelling is the first, reversible change. Karyorrhexis, karyolysis, a ruptured membrane, leaking contents, enzymatic digestion and necrosis with inflammation all mean the injury is irreversible.

hints.quote: Endometrial shedding in menstrual cycle - apoptosis (physiologic, programmed death)
hints.take: Apoptosis can be physiologic or pathologic and causes no inflammation; necrosis is always pathologic and brings inflammation.

hints.quote: Production of reactive oxygen species - mitochondrial respiration, reperfusion, respiratory burst in macrophages, ionizing radiation
hints.take: Know where free radicals come from and the three enzymes that remove them: superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase and catalase.

hints.quote: Metastatic carcinoma may cause increased calcium levels - calcium deposits in normal tissue
hints.take: Metastatic calcification: high serum calcium (bone destroyed by cancer, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, kidney failure) deposits in normal tissue. Dystrophic: normal calcium, damaged tissue (atheroma, damaged valves).

hints.quote: Immobilization - leads to atrophy of myocytes
hints.take: Know an example of each adaptation: disuse atrophy of skeletal muscle, hypertrophy of the heart in hypertension, hyperplasia (more cells, as in the prostate) and metaplasia (columnar to squamous in a smoker's bronchus). Anthracosis is carbon in the lung; alcohol makes a yellow fatty liver that can go on to cirrhosis.

hints.quote: Macrophages - slow response to activating stimuli, relying on new gene transcription
hints.take: Neutrophils are first and fast and live 1–2 days in tissue (degranulation, respiratory burst). Macrophages dominate chronic inflammation, live days to weeks (tissue-resident ones for years) and make nitric oxide and cytokines after new gene transcription.

hints.quote: Chronic inflammation - macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, tissue destruction and fibrosis (scarring)
hints.take: Acute: neutrophils, congestion and edema, tissue preserved, can resolve. Chronic: macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells, tissue destroyed and replaced by fibrosis, with loss of function.

hints.quote: Blister - serous inflammation
hints.take: Serous = cell-poor fluid (blister, effusion); fibrinous = fibrinogen leaks and fibrin coats the pericardium or pleura (adhesions if not cleared); purulent = neutrophils and liquefied debris, which can wall off into an abscess; ulcer = a surface defect from sloughed necrotic tissue.

hints.quote: Collagen - responsible for the tensile strength of a healed wound
hints.take: Granulation tissue (new vessels, fibroblasts, little collagen) comes first; collagen laid down in remodeling gives the scar its strength. A keloid is scar overgrowth past the wound's edges.

hints.quote: Most important clinical question for neoplasms
hints.take: Whether a tumor is benign or malignant sets the treatment: conservative or wide excision, lymph node staging, chemotherapy or radiation. Metastasis is the hallmark of malignancy; benign tumors are well differentiated, slow, often encapsulated and don't invade.

hints.quote: Not on the exam!
hints.take: Skip the step-by-step scheme of how SARS-CoV-2 replicates its genome and makes its mRNAs. Know that its genomic mRNA makes the ORF1a and ORF1b polyproteins (the replication proteins) and that its structural proteins come from subgenomic mRNAs.

hints.quote: Bacteria have different requirements for oxygen: obligate aerobes require oxygen to grow, whereas obligate anaerobes are killed in the presence of oxygen and facultative anaerobes can grow with or without oxygen.
hints.take: Obligate aerobes need O2 and can't ferment; facultative anaerobes respire with or without O2 or ferment; obligate anaerobes die in O2 because they lack superoxide dismutase and catalase to clear its radicals.

hints.quote: The bacterial growth curve has four main phases: lag, log, stationary, and death.
hints.take: Lag (adjusting), log (exponential division; antibiotics, which need growing cells, work best), stationary (nutrients run out; division equals death), death. Bacteria divide by binary fission, which needs new wall.

hints.quote: 38 ATP molecules are produced for every molecule of glucose that is broken down.
hints.take: Aerobic respiration (glycolysis, TCA cycle, electron transport at the plasma membrane, O2 as final acceptor) gives 38 ATP; anaerobic respiration ends on nitrate, sulfate or another acceptor and gives less; fermentation (glycolysis only, an organic acceptor) gives 2. Every route needs a final acceptor to regenerate NAD+ and FAD.

hints.quote: Genetic recombination occurs in bacteria through transformation, transduction, or conjugation.
hints.take: Transformation = naked DNA (a competent cell; rare); transduction = a phage (generalized: random genes; specialized: genes beside the prophage); conjugation = a sex pilus, one plasmid strand passes and the F− cell becomes F+. Each can make a bacterium more virulent or resistant.

hints.quote: Note: Ergosterol is part of the plasma membrane not the cell wall!
hints.take: Ergosterol is in the fungal plasma membrane: polyenes bind it, and azoles and terbinafine block its synthesis. The wall is chitin, β-glucans and mannoproteins; echinocandins block glucan.

hints.quote: Thermal Dimorphism: Seen in true fungal pathogens, allowing growth as molds in the environment (saprobic phase) and as yeasts in the host (parasitic phase).
hints.take: Thermal dimorphism marks the true (endemic) pathogens, Histoplasma, Blastomyces and Coccidioides: mold in the soil, yeast in the body. Most opportunists aren't dimorphic.

hints.quote: not "Gram-positive"!
hints.take: M. tuberculosis is found with the acid-fast stain (red fuchsin, acid alcohol, methylene blue): its lipid-rich, mycolic-acid envelope doesn't take the gram stain reliably.

hints.quote: Applies to all future drugs!
hints.take: A cavity holds about 10^9 bacilli and resistance to any one drug arises in 1 in 10^5–10^8, so TB is always treated with several drugs at once: four for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4.

hints.quote: Questions in exam will have only one right answer designed to test very basic knowledge of how these tests can be used in a diagnostic setting for pathogen ID
hints.take: Match each test to what it finds: acid-fast stain (TB), KOH, PAS and silver (fungi), India ink (Cryptococcus), dark-field (T. pallidum), serology (hard-to-grow organisms such as Rickettsia and Mycoplasma), antigen tests, the PPD skin test (TB) and PCR (chlamydia and gonorrhea).

hints.quote: will only test on examples provided in lecture
hints.take: For bacterial virulence, know the lecture's own examples; in this part: M. tuberculosis blocking phagolysosome maturation (the granuloma), Rickettsia in endothelium (vasculitis, DIC) and the clostridial toxins (alpha toxin, tetanus, botulinum).

hints.quote: Important enzyme inhibitors and inducers to know
hints.take: Inhibitors raise other drugs' levels: grapefruit juice, ketoconazole and fluconazole, clarithromycin. Inducers lower them: St. John's wort, rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, cigarette smoking.

hints.quote: Common terms to know: Indication, dosing, contraindication, side/adverse effects, poison
hints.take: An indication is an approved reason to use a drug and a contraindication (relative or absolute) a reason not to; a side effect is an unintended effect of the drug, while an adverse event is any harm during or after use, caused by the drug or not; a poison has almost only harmful effects.

hints.quote: Generic name (nonproprietary) (Name used in Board Exams)
hints.take: Learn every drug by its generic name (acetaminophen, atorvastatin), not its trade name (Tylenol, Lipitor).

hints.quote: it is important to note that there is no change in the actual lengths of the thick and thin filaments between rest and contraction
hints.take: Contraction is the filaments sliding: their overlap grows and the I and H bands narrow, but neither filament shortens, so the A band keeps its length.

hints.quote: It is important to note the difference in the thickness of the tunica media layer between the arterial and venous sides of the cardiovascular system.
hints.take: Arteries and arterioles have a thick smooth-muscle tunica media (a high wall-to-lumen ratio); veins and venules have a thin media, and their thickest layer is the tunica externa.

hints.quote: IE prophylaxis: prosthetic valves, prior IE – amoxicillin 2g before invasive dental procedure
hints.take: Prophylaxis is for the highest-risk hearts only: a prosthetic valve or valve repair material, past endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and a heart transplant with valve disease. Amoxicillin 2 g by mouth 30–60 minutes before a procedure that manipulates the gingiva or the periapical tissue. Rheumatic heart disease, mitral valve prolapse or a murmur alone doesn't qualify.

hints.quote: Atherosclerosis underpins most CV disease – risk factors are on nearly every patient intake form
hints.take: Know the risk factors (hypertension, high LDL, diabetes, smoking, obesity, inactivity, family history) and the steps: endothelial injury, oxidized LDL taken up by macrophages as foam cells (the fatty streak), a fibrous plaque, then rupture and a thrombus (MI or stroke).

hints.quote: Important drugs to know
hints.take: One drug per class: IA procainamide, IB lidocaine, IC flecainide; II esmolol, metoprolol; III amiodarone; IV verapamil, diltiazem; others digoxin and magnesium sulfate.

hints.quote: Summary of Key Points
hints.take: Front-line for hypertension: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers and thiazides. Cough and angioedema are the ACE inhibitors' own (bradykinin); both RAAS classes cause high K+ and kidney injury and harm the fetus; CCBs cause gingival overgrowth; thiazides lower Na+ and K+ and are sulfonamides.

hints.quote: Remember that primary hemostasis is a platelet or vessel disorder. Secondary hemostasis involves the coagulation cascade.
hints.take: Mucosal oozing, petechiae and bleeding from small cuts point to platelets or vessels (von Willebrand disease, low platelets, aspirin); delayed, deep and joint bleeding points to a clotting factor (hemophilia, warfarin, liver disease).

hints.quote: The thing to keep in mind is that there are mechanisms in place to keep the coagulation cascade in place. If these are missing, then a hypercoagulable (thrombotic) state is the result.
hints.take: A lack of protein C, protein S or antithrombin, or factor V Leiden or prothrombin G20210A, tips the balance toward clots, not bleeding.

hints.quote: The fine details are not necessary to remember.
hints.take: Skip how blood is collected for clotting tests (the citrate tube and its blood-to-citrate ratio); know that the PT follows the extrinsic pathway (III and VII, "37 cents") and the aPTT the intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII, "$11.98").

hints.quote: You should know the following equations
hints.take: Capacities are sums of volumes: inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV; vital capacity = IC + ERV (IRV + TV + ERV); FRC = ERV + RV; TLC = VC + RV. Anything that contains RV needs helium dilution or plethysmography.

hints.quote: the fundamental relationship in respiratory physiology
hints.take: The alveolar ventilation equation: alveolar PCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation. Halve ventilation and PaCO2 doubles; double CO2 production and ventilation must double to hold PaCO2 at 40 mmHg.

hints.quote: Remember these values!
hints.take: Humidified inspired air: PO2 about 145 mmHg (760 × 19.7%) and PCO2 about 0. Against mixed venous blood (PO2 40, PCO2 45), they set the gradients that bring alveolar gas and arterial blood to 100 and 40.

hints.quote: The much more important point is an understanding of the dermatomes
hints.take: Thoracic dermatomes: T2 at the sternal angle, T4 at the nipple, T10 at the umbilicus. The intercostal nerves are T1–T11 and the subcostal nerve T12; the names of their cutaneous branches matter less.

hints.quote: Don't need to remember all these values but keep in mind as we move along that oxygen is much higher than CO2.
hints.take: Skip the percentages of nitrogen, oxygen, argon and CO2 in air; know that air holds far more O2 than CO2 (inspired PCO2 is about 0).

hints.quote: It is not necessary to memorize all of the groups
hints.take: Skip the names of the lymph node groups around the trachea and lungs; know only that they exist and are named by where they sit.

hints.quote: Sarcoidosis is the most high-yield for both specialties – often undiagnosed at the first encounter
hints.take: Sarcoidosis: noncaseating granulomas, high ACE and calcium, young adults and African American women; in the mouth, parotid and gingival enlargement and radiolucent jaw lesions; Heerfordt syndrome = parotid enlargement + uveitis + facial nerve palsy.

hints.quote: Strawberry gingivitis + sinusitis + renal disease = GPA
hints.take: Red, granular, friable gingival overgrowth with sinusitis and kidney disease is granulomatosis with polyangiitis: biopsy and refer, don't treat it as periodontitis.

hints.quote: Reversible (key distinction from COPD)
hints.take: Asthma's obstruction reverses with a bronchodilator; COPD's (chronic bronchitis plus emphysema) doesn't.

hints.quote: Important drugs to know
hints.take: Sinusitis and otitis media: amoxicillin or amoxicillin–clavulanate. Influenza: oseltamivir, zanamivir, amantadine, rimantadine, baloxavir. Bronchitis: azithromycin, clarithromycin, TMP-SMX. Pneumonia: doxycycline, levofloxacin, vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam. TB: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol.

hints.quote: Important drugs to know
hints.take: First-generation H1 blockers (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) cross the blood–brain barrier and block muscarinic and alpha receptors, so they sedate; second generation (cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine) barely do; topical: azelastine, olopatadine, ketotifen. Epinephrine for anaphylaxis is given by injection, never by mouth.

hints.quote: It is CRITICAL that you understand these four terms. They will be used 100x throughout the module
hints.take: Filtration (glomerulus into Bowman space), reabsorption (tubule back to the blood), secretion (blood into the tubule) and excretion (urine): excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.

hints.quote: This is a really important relationship.
hints.take: Each nephron's distal tubule comes back to touch its own glomerulus: the macula densa, where the thick ascending limb meets the DCT, lies against the renin-making JG cells of the afferent arteriole (the juxtaglomerular apparatus).

hints.quote: Make sure you know the terms here.
hints.take: Total body water, ICF, ECF, plasma and interstitial fluid, and the 60–40–20 rule: 42, 28 and 14 L in a 70-kg adult.

hints.quote: you should understand how the common IV solutions alter the volume and osmolarities of the ECF and ICF
hints.take: 0.9% saline expands only the ECF; 0.45% saline lowers osmolarity and moves some water into cells; D5W is free water that expands both compartments the most.

hints.quote: It is imperative that you know the parts of a nephron.
hints.take: Know the nephron in order (renal corpuscle, proximal tubule, thin descending, thin ascending and thick ascending limbs, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct) and the four processes: filtered − reabsorbed + secreted = excreted.

hints.quote: so we need to know this pathway
hints.take: Urine: collecting duct → papilla (the tip of a pyramid) → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder. Blood: renal → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular arteries → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries.

hints.quote: I will call it 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol if you have it on the test
hints.take: Active vitamin D is made in the kidney: 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, by 1α-hydroxylase, turned on by low Ca2+, high PTH and low phosphate; 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol is inactive.

hints.quote: the word I want you to remember with this is the Pontine Micturition Center … it's a relatively simple pathway. But there will be a question or two on there.
hints.take: Bladder stretch at about 300 mL sets off a spinal reflex; the pontine micturition center holds it back or lets voiding go ahead (pudendal inhibited so the external sphincter relaxes; parasympathetic contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter). Sympathetic stores; parasympathetic voids.

hints.quote: So it's important that you know that JG cells contain renin.
hints.take: JG (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall hold renin; macula densa cells sense NaCl and release adenosine, which constricts the afferent arteriole (tubuloglomerular feedback); a sustained change brings renin release.

hints.quote: This slide's imperative that you understand it, because the next five slides are building on this slide
hints.take: GFR = Kf × [(glomerular capillary hydrostatic − Bowman space hydrostatic) − glomerular capillary oncotic pressure]; Bowman space oncotic pressure is about 0. The class numbers: 45 − 10 − 19 = 16 mmHg.

hints.quote: Put a star next to this. They do not have the same effect on the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillary.
hints.take: Constricting either arteriole lowers renal plasma flow; afferent constriction lowers glomerular pressure and GFR, efferent constriction raises them.

hints.quote: If nothing else, if you can get yourself through this, you're good, okay? You're good, because questions will be kind of based on that.
hints.take: Know the What changes GFR table: afferent constriction, RPF and GFR down; efferent constriction, RPF down and GFR up; a blocked ureter, GFR down with RPF unchanged; plasma protein up, GFR down; plasma protein down, GFR up.

hints.quote: Plasma creatinine concentration varies inversely with GFR.
hints.take: At steady state, double the plasma creatinine means half the GFR. Creatinine slightly overestimates GFR because a little is secreted; inulin is the gold standard.

hints.quote: So there's 2 examples of C is equal to 0 that I want you to know.
hints.take: Albumin (not filtered) and glucose (filtered, then all reabsorbed) have a clearance of 0; PAH's clearance is the highest possible, equal to renal plasma flow.

hints.quote: The major cation of extracellular fluid is sodium. You have to know this.
hints.take: ECF: Na+ the main cation, Cl− the main anion and HCO3− second. ICF: K+, then Mg2+, with organic phosphates and proteins as the anions.

hints.quote: What I want you to know is that the normal osmolarity of body fluids is 275 to 290 milliosmoles per kilogram.
hints.take: Normal osmolarity is 275–290 mOsm/kg, the same inside and outside cells; estimate plasma osmolarity as 2[Na+] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8.

hints.quote: water will shift across the cell membranes to make the osmolarity on both sides the same … It's very important that you understand that concept.
hints.take: Every gain or loss happens in the ECF first; if ECF osmolarity changes, water moves into or out of cells until ICF and ECF osmolarity match again.

hints.quote: You are going to see these images, these exact ones … on your test
hints.take: Read a Darrow-Yannet diagram (ICF left, ECF right; width is volume, height is osmolarity; dashed line the new state). Diarrhea: ECF smaller, same height. Sweating: both smaller, higher. Adrenal insufficiency: ECF smaller, ICF larger, lower. Saline: ECF larger, same. Salt: ECF larger, ICF smaller, higher. SIADH: both larger, lower.

hints.quote: there's no math on the test. Okay, there's no math. I'm not going to ask you to really calculate anything. I may ask you for, like, a percentage of something
hints.take: Know what the clearance, osmolarity and Starling equations mean and which way each term moves things; the worked numbers in this part are practice for that, not arithmetic to drill.

hints.quote: I don't really care about the stripes … so don't worry about the stripes as much.
hints.take: Skip the outer medulla's stripes; know the cortex, outer medulla and inner medulla, and that short loops stay in the outer medulla while long loops reach the inner medulla.

hints.quote: I do not want you to even look at that box with the connecting things, because we don't know what those are, and it doesn't matter.
hints.take: Skip the slit diaphragm's proteins; know the barrier's three layers (fenestrated endothelium, negatively charged basement membrane, podocyte foot processes) and that it holds back large, negative proteins.

hints.quote: I don't think these nerves are mentioned on the test, but I'll tell you if they are later on.
hints.take: Skip the names of the pelvic and hypogastric nerves that carry the bladder's stretch signal; know what sympathetic, parasympathetic and pudendal (somatic) activity each do to the detrusor and the two sphincters.

hints.quote: I do not believe there's any hematocrit and sodium questions on the test
hints.take: Skip the hematocrit and plasma Na+ columns of the fluid-shift summary; know what happens to ECF volume, ICF volume and osmolarity.

hints.quote: This is an excellent summary of where the various filtered solutes and water are reabsorbed along the nephron
hints.take: Know each segment's share. Na+: proximal tubule about 65%, loop 25%, DCT 5%, collecting duct 4–5%. Water: proximal tubule about 65%, thin descending limb 10%, collecting duct about 5% to more than 24% with ADH.

hints.quote: this is like so important, I can't overemphasize it enough because you're going to see probably 15 to 20 images of cells
hints.take: For every cell drawing, find the apical (lumen) side and the basolateral (blood) side with its Na+-K+-ATPase, then ask whether each solute is reabsorbed or secreted and whether it crosses through the cell or between cells.

hints.quote: Proximal tubule reabsorbs a lot, is the take-home message.
hints.take: The proximal tubule takes back about two-thirds of filtered water, Na+ and Cl− and nearly all glucose, HCO3− and amino acids, iso-osmotically.

hints.quote: the take-home thing here is that there's a limited number of transporters in the apical membrane … That means that the mechanism is saturable and it has a transport maximum.
hints.take: SGLT2 (apical) and GLUT (basolateral) reabsorb all filtered glucose until the carriers saturate: glycosuria starts at about 180–200 mg/dL (splay), and all carriers are full (Tm) above about 350 mg/dL.

hints.quote: Flozins affect the proximal convoluted tubule. Specifically, they're targeting this SGLT2
hints.take: The flozins (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin) block SGLT2 in the apical membrane of the proximal tubule, causing glycosuria; SGLT1 in the gut is untouched.

hints.quote: If you can wrap your head around this graph, you're in good shape.
hints.take: Along the proximal tubule, tubular fluid ÷ plasma for Na+ stays about 1 (iso-osmotic); glucose, amino acids and HCO3− fall toward 0; Cl− rises, because HCO3− is taken first, until the late segment takes Cl− back.

hints.quote: Volume expansion leads to decreased reabsorption. … Volume contraction leads to increased reabsorption. If you know that, you're good to go.
hints.take: ECF volume expansion lowers proximal reabsorption (peritubular hydrostatic pressure up, oncotic pressure down); contraction raises it. With glomerulotubular balance, a rise in GFR raises proximal reabsorption so the fraction stays about the same.

hints.quote: I really want you to put a star by the descending limb … is permeable to water. But the ascending limb is not
hints.take: Thin descending limb: water out (and urea in), so the fluid concentrates. Thin and thick ascending limbs: no water; NaCl leaves, so the fluid dilutes (the TAL through NKCC2: the diluting segment).

hints.quote: whether we go to 600 or go to 1200 depends on whether or not we have antidiuretic hormone present
hints.take: The corticopapillary gradient runs from 300 mOsm/kg to about 600 at the papilla without ADH and up to about 1,200 with it; ADH raises NKCC2 activity in the TAL and water and urea permeability in the collecting duct.

hints.quote: here's the take home message right here. When you have ADH present
hints.take: ADH puts aquaporins into the outer and inner medullary collecting ducts and urea transporters into the inner medullary duct only; urea concentrates in the duct, leaves into the inner medulla and recycles into the thin descending limb.

hints.quote: multiple nephrons that connect to a singular collecting duct. Okay, that's important. That's a test question.
hints.take: Several nephrons drain into one collecting duct: their connecting tubules merge at the cortical collecting duct (how many per duct doesn't matter).

hints.quote: It's probably going to say like thin descending limb, thin ascending limb, thick ascending limb. It's probably going to be more specific, right? And then what does it block?
hints.take: Name each diuretic's exact segment and target: acetazolamide, carbonic anhydrase (proximal tubule); loop diuretics, NKCC2 (thick ascending limb); thiazides, NCC (distal convoluted tubule); amiloride and triamterene, ENaC, and spironolactone, the aldosterone receptor (principal cells).

hints.quote: Really, this is going to be questions on, like, channels and where they're located and what they're doing
hints.take: For each channel know its side, cell and segment: SGLT2 apical and GLUT basolateral (proximal tubule); NKCC2 apical (TAL); NCC and TRPV5 apical (DCT); ENaC and ROMK apical (principal cells); H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase apical, AE1 basolateral (α-intercalated); pendrin apical (β-intercalated).

hints.quote: It responds to external signals and hormones. Star.
hints.take: The collecting duct reabsorbs only about 4–5% of filtered Na+ but is the segment hormones tune: principal cells respond to aldosterone (more ENaC and Na+-K+-ATPase) and ADH (aquaporin-2).

hints.quote: these alpha intercalated cells, make sure you know that
hints.take: α-intercalated cells secrete H+ (apical H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase, which takes K+ back) and return HCO3− to the blood through basolateral AE1; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO3− through apical pendrin.

hints.quote: You do not need to know the specifics in the diagram.
hints.take: Skip the anatomy in the hypothalamus diagram; know where ADH is made, where the osmoreceptors are and that hyperosmolarity releases ADH and stimulates thirst.

hints.quote: You do need to know: ADH is produced in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei in the hypothalamus.
hints.take: ADH is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei; the OVLT and subfornical organ send axons to them and to the cortex's thirst areas (insula, anterior cingulate gyrus); hyperosmolarity releases ADH and stimulates thirst.

hints.quote: So the take-home story is that ADH release occurs before the stimulation of the thirst response.
hints.take: A 1–2% rise in plasma osmolarity releases ADH; thirst needs about 2–3%, so the kidney starts saving water before you feel thirsty.

hints.quote: Again, the take-home message is that pressure changes are more important than osmolarity changes.
hints.take: Volume wins: a 5–10% fall in blood volume or pressure releases ADH even when the plasma is dilute.

hints.quote: Levels in these patients are consistently high, okay, they're consistently high, so that's really the take-home point here
hints.take: In SIADH, ADH stays high and unregulated (often from a tumor such as small cell lung cancer): water is kept, sodium falls and the urine is inappropriately concentrated.

hints.quote: it's not going to be that granular, okay, it's going to be more like globally, why would hypernatremia or why would hyponatremia result
hints.take: Skip the long lists of causes of hypo- and hypernatremia; know why each happens: too much water for the sodium, or too little.

hints.quote: this kind of grayed-out text right here, I will not test you on
hints.take: Skip how the ADH precursor is packaged and cleaved on its way down the axon; know where ADH is made and released.

hints.quote: You do not have to memorize all of these, okay? I'm not gonna say, like, central DI is caused by all of the following, except
hints.take: Skip the full lists of causes of central and nephrogenic DI; know the big picture: too little ADH (central) versus kidneys that ignore it (nephrogenic, most often lithium), and how each is treated.

hints.quote: Stimulates renin release. You have to know this for the test, it's gonna be a question, right?
hints.take: Renin is released for low perfusion pressure in the afferent arteriole, sympathetic β1 stimulation and low NaCl at the macula densa (signaled by prostaglandins).

hints.quote: you should put your money on inhibition.
hints.take: ANP inhibits: renin, aldosterone, ADH and Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct all go down, so Na+ and water are excreted.

hints.quote: this is where you need to put your star. The excessive fluid is a result of sodium and water retention in the interstitial compartment.
hints.take: In heart failure the extra fluid is interstitial, where the baroreceptors can't sense it; the effective circulating volume is low, so the kidney keeps retaining Na+.

hints.quote: If there's ECF volume depletion, the baroreceptors will stimulate renal sympathetic activity. That's the big take-home.
hints.take: Low volume → baroreceptors → renal sympathetic nerves: the arterioles constrict, renin is released and Na+ reabsorption rises.

hints.quote: if you can wrap your head around this, you're going to be in pretty good shape
hints.take: Know the K+ shift table: insulin, β2 agonists, α blockers, alkalosis and aldosterone move K+ into cells; insulin deficiency, β-blockers, α agonists, acidosis, hyperosmolarity, cell lysis and hard exercise move it out.

hints.quote: Much of the effect of aldosterone on potassium secretion is secondary to its effect on sodium reabsorption.
hints.take: Aldosterone adds ENaC channels; more Na+ reabsorbed makes the lumen more negative and drives K+ secretion.

hints.quote: I'm not going to mention like [Liddle] syndrome and try to quiz you on, like, what's going on with that.
hints.take: Skip the rare causes of hypokalemia such as Liddle syndrome; know the big causes: K+ shifting into cells, renal loss (diuretics, excess aldosterone) and low intake.

hints.quote: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin production, okay? So just go ahead and circle that for me.
hints.take: NSAIDs block the macula densa's prostaglandins, so renin and aldosterone fall and K+ is retained: in CKD this causes hyperkalemia, so these patients limit K+ and avoid NSAIDs.

hints.quote: I'm not going to ask you to remember like transporters and stuff like that. We're thinking big picture, we're thinking how things are moving
hints.take: Skip the names of the Ca2+, Mg2+ and phosphate channels and transporters; know where along the nephron each ion is reabsorbed and what moves it (paracellular in the proximal tubule and TAL, PTH and thiazides in the DCT).

hints.quote: Loop diuretics will excrete more calcium, thiazide diuretics, you hold on to calcium.
hints.take: Loop diuretics remove the TAL's lumen-positive voltage, so Ca2+ and Mg2+ are lost in the urine; thiazides lower Ca2+ excretion.

hints.quote: Henderson-Hasselbalch? I'm not too concerned about it, but the important thing here is that when we use this Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, we get a ratio of bicarbonate to carbon dioxide levels.
hints.take: Skip the equation itself; know that pH follows the ratio of HCO3− to CO2: more HCO3− raises it, more CO2 lowers it.

hints.quote: Again, mechanism not too important, but again, pay attention to this calcium exchange here, or not calcium, potassium exchange
hints.take: Skip the details of ammonia handling in the collecting duct; know that acidosis drives K+ out of cells (hyperkalemia) and alkalosis drives it in.

hints.quote: When the arrows are in the same directions, it's a metabolic change.
hints.take: Compare arrows: PCO2 and HCO3− moving opposite to the pH means a respiratory disorder; moving the same way as the pH means a metabolic one.

hints.quote: Right, so you have to fix fluid volume first, and then everything can restore.
hints.take: A vomiting (contraction) alkalosis lasts while the patient is volume depleted, because angiotensin II and aldosterone keep HCO3− high; rehydration lets it correct.

hints.quote: No need to memorize values! Let’s mark them as elevated or decreased.
hints.take: Skip the renal lab table's cutoffs by stage; know which way each moves as the kidneys fail: BUN, creatinine and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio rise, GFR and creatinine clearance fall.

hints.quote: No need to memorize these. Note there are many signs and symptoms of CKD.
hints.take: Skip the system-by-system list of uremic signs; know that uremia touches nearly every system, and learn the oral and eye signs of CKD.

hints.quote: So the histologic hallmark, and you should know this, is that you're going to see epithelial crescents.
hints.take: Rapidly progressive GN: crescents of epithelial cells in Bowman space and loss of function over days to weeks; most patients end up on dialysis or with a transplant.

hints.quote: Say, if you had this on a test, someone would tell you this is the IgA, immunofluorescence, and then they would ask you, what diagnosis is that?
hints.take: Mesangial IgA on immunofluorescence is IgA nephropathy (Berger disease): recurrent hematuria a day or two after a respiratory infection.

hints.quote: And this is one of the reasons that we actually go over the different layers of the glomerulus, so you can really appreciate, where this specific injury is occurring
hints.take: Know where each deposit sits: subepithelial (membranous spikes, post-streptococcal humps), subendothelial (MPGN type I), mesangial (IgA), linear along the GBM (anti-GBM); none in minimal change disease.

hints.quote: Just sort of be aware that it exists, but we're not going to go, into, much detail on that.
hints.take: Interstitial nephritis: know only that it is inflammation around the tubules, from drugs or infection.

hints.quote: Okay, but we're not going to go into much detail, or any other detail on that.
hints.take: Acute tubular necrosis: know only that the tubular cells die, usually after ischemia or a toxin.

hints.quote: you don't have to know this really in any detail, but we divide things up into pre-renal, renal, and post-renal causes of kidney failures.
hints.take: Know only that kidney failure can be pre-renal, renal or post-renal; the lecture's diseases are the renal causes.

hints.quote: It's not super important, to, to kind of, to know this
hints.take: Skip the classification of kidney diseases into groups; learn the diseases themselves.

hints.quote: just kind of be aware that these syndromes, exist
hints.take: Skip the syndromes that link the kidney and the eye; know the common oral and eye signs of kidney disease instead.

hints.quote: And so this is one of the take-homes that I want you to take.
hints.take: Know the oral signs of kidney disease (pale mucosa, petechiae and ecchymoses, uremic stomatitis, periodontal disease, altered taste, xerostomia; enamel hypoplasia and delayed eruption in children) and the eye signs (diabetic retinopathy, macular degeneration, glaucoma, cataracts).

hints.quote: I'm not going to test you on reference ranges because nowadays on every lab test you ever run ... you'll have reference ranges on there
hints.take: Skip normal lab values (BUN, serum creatinine, creatinine clearance): the lab report prints them. Know which way each moves as the kidneys fail, the eGFR stage cutoffs (90, 60, 30, 15) and the albuminuria categories (under 30, 30–300, over 300 mg/g), which are stages, not reference ranges.

hints.quote: Note these.
hints.take: Know the oral signs of CKD: uremic stomatitis, xerostomia, taste changes, mucosal petechiae and ecchymoses, pale mucosa from anemia, mucosal lesions, periodontal disease and renal osteodystrophy (demineralized jaws that can fracture during treatment); and the eye signs: retinopathy, glaucoma and cataracts.

hints.quote: Maybe life in general, know where they're working and kind of what they are, what co-transport they are targeting.
hints.take: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the TAL; thiazides block NCC in the DCT; K+-sparing drugs act on the collecting duct's principal cells (ENaC or the aldosterone receptor).

hints.quote: But you do really need to understand how diuretics are going to alter sodium and water handling, because this is going to impact your patient's presentation
hints.take: Diuretic patients: orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, bathroom breaks, cramps and low K+ (loop, thiazide) or high K+ (K+-sparing).

hints.quote: the biggest thing is you have to avoid NSAIDs. Do not prescribe ibuprofen or Aleve, to these patients
hints.take: In kidney disease, no NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): acetaminophen is the analgesic, with opioids such as codeine, hydrocodone or tramadol at the lowest dose.

hints.quote: Metronidazole is safe to use.
hints.take: Clindamycin, azithromycin and metronidazole usually need no dose change in kidney failure; amoxicillin, penicillin VK and cephalexin get longer intervals.

hints.quote: So the day after dialysis is the best time to treat a patient.
hints.take: Treat a hemodialysis patient the day after dialysis: the heparin has worn off and fluid and electrolytes are at their best.

hints.quote: Immunosuppressive therapy effects, you should know what those are.
hints.take: Transplant immunosuppressants: infection, candidiasis, slow healing, cyclosporine gingival overgrowth, more oral cancer, and adrenal suppression from steroids.

hints.quote: You're going to see a lot of patients with hypertension and diabetes-related kidney disease, so those are the things that I would focus a good bit of my energy on
hints.take: Diabetic kidney disease: periodontal disease, infection and slow healing, glucose control. Hypertensive kidney disease: blood pressure every visit, careful epinephrine, no NSAIDs.

hints.quote: It is important to note, that the small intestine, the section of the GI tract in which the majority of the nutrients, electrolytes and water are absorbed, is the region where the luminal surface is elaborated into villi. In contrast the large intestine lacks the villi.
hints.take: The small intestine, where most nutrients, electrolytes and water are absorbed, is lined with villi (with plicae and microvilli, about 600 times the area of a plain tube); the colon has no villi.

hints.quote: Remember that segmental propulsion is the formation of moving pockets of chyme in the small intestine by constriction of the circular muscle, with the segmentation contracting in the middle of the bolus of chyme, whereas in peristaltic propulsion: contraction takes place behind the bolus of chyme & relaxation ahead of it.
hints.take: Segmentation contracts the circular muscle in the middle of the bolus and mixes; peristalsis contracts behind the bolus and relaxes ahead of it, and propels.

hints.quote: CRITICAL POINT: The pancreaticoduodenal arteries are the only anastomosis between the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery.
hints.take: The superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (celiac, through the gastroduodenal) meet the inferior ones (SMA) around the head of the pancreas, the one celiac–SMA link. The marginal artery is the SMA–IMA link.

hints.quote: CRITICAL POINT: Under normal conditions (i.e. when pressures are equal across the two systems), very little blood flows across these anastomotic connections.
hints.take: Portal-caval anastomoses (esophagus, umbilicus, rectum) carry almost nothing until portal pressure rises, as in cirrhosis; then they dilate into esophageal varices, caput medusae and rectal varices.

hints.quote: Note that the portal system is ventral to the caval system. This is a very important point for cross sectional anatomy and radiography.
hints.take: On a cross section or scan, the anterior of the two large veins is the portal vein and the posterior one the IVC.

hints.quote: This is a favorite exam distinction: Meissner = Mucosal functions (secretion), whereas Auerbach = Action (motility).
hints.take: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus runs secretion and local blood flow; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, between the circular and longitudinal muscle, runs peristalsis.

hints.quote: Exam pearl: centroacinar cells = pancreas, striated ducts = salivary gland.
hints.take: Pancreatic acini have centroacinar cells (the start of the intercalated duct) and no striated ducts or myoepithelial cells; salivary glands have striated ducts and myoepithelial cells.

hints.quote: The major point is to keep blood, bile, and lymph in separate spaces.
hints.take: Blood runs in the sinusoids to the central vein; bile in canaliculi between hepatocytes out to the portal bile ducts; lymph in the space of Disse out to portal lymphatics.

hints.quote: highest-yield for their boards and their chair-side practice: oral and ocular manifestations, viral hepatitis transmission and infection control, and hepatic drug metabolism
hints.take: Know the oral signs of liver disease and their causes (jaundice, bleeding and petechiae, fetor hepaticus, smooth tongue, xerostomia; oral lichen planus is a reason to ask about hepatitis C), how each hepatitis virus spreads and how the team is protected, and which dental drugs the liver clears.

hints.quote: Hepatitis B - HIGH-YIELD occupational risk.
hints.take: About 1.5% of dental patients carry hepatitis B: vaccinate the whole team, use standard precautions, have a post-exposure plan, and read the serology (HBsAg infected, IgM anti-HBc acute, IgG anti-HBc past or chronic, anti-HBs immune).

hints.quote: HIGH-YIELD prescribing slide.
hints.take: The liver clears amide local anesthetics, aspirin, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, codeine, meperidine, diazepam, barbiturates, erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline, ketoconazole and fluconazole. In significant liver disease lower the doses, lengthen the intervals, respect local anesthetic maximums and avoid the agents the slide marks (erythromycin, clindamycin and tetracycline; halothane and thiopental).

hints.quote: Acetaminophen - the one to fear.
hints.take: Acetaminophen causes about 46% of acute liver failure, most of it accidental; N-acetylcysteine works best in the first 8–10 hours, and every product a patient already takes counts toward the daily total.

hints.quote: we are not asking dental and optometry students to read biopsies; the histology slides are for pattern recognition and vocabulary only
hints.take: Learn the words for each liver injury pattern and what each means (ballooning, acidophil bodies, steatosis, bridging fibrosis, regenerative nodules, Mallory-Denk bodies); reading a liver biopsy image isn't expected.

hints.quote: Keep brief - name recognition and the obstructive-jaundice link are enough.
hints.take: Cholangiocarcinoma: know that it is an adenocarcinoma of the bile ducts that shows late, with obstructive jaundice.

hints.quote: Several refs differ re: receptors in CTZ and STN (not important)
hints.take: Know each antiemetic's receptor (H1 and muscarinic for motion sickness, D2, 5-HT3) and its side effects, not which brainstem site (chemoreceptor trigger zone or solitary tract nucleus) holds which receptor.

hints.quote: Methotrexate is associated with a high incidence of mucositis and stomatitis which can be diminished by supplementation with folic acid
hints.take: Methotrexate (used for Crohn disease) causes mucositis and aphthous stomatitis; folic acid lowers it, and NSAIDs slow its elimination.

hints.quote: Crohn's disease can present with oral lesions before intestinal symptoms appear.
hints.take: Cobblestoning, diffuse mucosal or lip swelling, aphthous-like ulcers and orofacial granulomatosis can be the first sign of Crohn disease: document them and coordinate care with the physician or gastroenterologist.

hints.quote: GERD commonly produces dental erosion on lingual maxillary surfaces.
hints.take: Smooth, shiny erosion of the palatal surfaces of the maxillary teeth, with posterior occlusal cupping and sensitivity, points to reflux: refer for medical care, give fluoride and advise on diet and brushing times.

hints.quote: It's gonna cover the 8 major themes of the course.
hints.take: Learn the eight: anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia, asthma, chest pain, syncope, stroke, seizure and aspiration, each with its signs, first steps and drug.

hints.quote: you never want to be the one to stop the blood thinner
hints.take: The prescriber decides about stopping an anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug; you consult, use local hemostasis and document.

hints.quote: now it's circulation airway breathing
hints.take: BLS is C-A-B: a 10-second breathing and pulse check, then compressions first.

hints.quote: That's probably one for the test
hints.take: Head tilt-chin lift opens the airway because lifting the mandible pulls the genioglossus and the tongue off the back of the throat.

hints.quote: do you put in the ankle? Do you put in the thigh?
hints.take: IM epinephrine goes into the thigh (anterolateral); know the site broadly, not to the inch.

hints.quote: This is always very testable
hints.take: Mallampati classes I to IV by what you see; III and IV predict a difficult airway.

hints.quote: a question that's going to show up on like every board exam
hints.take: Aspirated objects go to the right main bronchus: wider, shorter and more vertical.

hints.quote: don't do the blind finger sweep
hints.take: A blind sweep pushes the object deeper; remove only what you can see.

hints.quote: It's never wrong to call EMS early.
hints.take: EMS takes about 7 minutes or more; call as soon as an airway problem isn't resolving.

hints.quote: A common thing that shows up on exams
hints.take: Laryngospasm is more likely in a lightly sedated patient than in one deeply asleep.

hints.quote: Almost all bleeding can be stopped with gauze under pressure.
hints.take: Firm, direct pressure on folded gauze over the socket for 10–15 minutes comes before anything else.

hints.quote: What we want you guys to focus on really will be the management, and more importantly, the workup.
hints.take: Know who is at risk, which drugs matter and what you do in the office, more than the pathophysiology.

hints.quote: you are still the main provider
hints.take: A physician's opinion doesn't shift responsibility: follow the standard of care and document whom you spoke with.

hints.quote: I would rather deal with the bleeding
hints.take: Most patients stay on their anticoagulant or antiplatelet for simple extractions; you control bleeding locally.

hints.quote: Learn that number. Have it in your mind.
hints.take: Hypoglycemia (the lecture's number): serum glucose under about 50–60 mg/dL, with confusion, seizures and coma.

hints.quote: this is the information that you need to know
hints.take: Rule of twos: 20 mg of hydrocortisone (or equivalent) daily, for 2 weeks or more, within 2 years.

hints.quote: No more than five.
