hn-neck: Sympathetic = T1–L2 lateral horn; head fibers synapse in the superior cervical ganglion and ride the carotid arteries.
Parasympathetic head ganglia: ciliary (III), pterygopalatine and submandibular (VII), otic (IX).
Horner: partial ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, flushing (Pancoast tumor).
CN XI is superficial in the posterior triangle: injury = drooped shoulder, weak shrug.
Great auricular (C2–C3) supplies skin over the angle of the mandible, not V3.
Hyoid C3, thyroid cartilage C4–C5, cricoid C6.
ECA: SALFOPSM; ICA has no branches in the neck.
Carotid sinus = baroreceptor, carotid body = chemoreceptor, both via IX.
Carotid sheath: carotid medial, IJV lateral, X behind; sympathetic trunk outside, behind.
Phrenic C3–5 on the anterior scalene; thoracic duct ends at the left venous angle.
Superior thyroid a. + external laryngeal n. (pitch); inferior thyroid a. + recurrent laryngeal n. (hoarseness).
Danger space (alar–prevertebral) runs to the diaphragm: route to the mediastinum.
hn-skull: Pterion = frontal, parietal, temporal, sphenoid; over the anterior branch of the MMA.
Epidural = MMA, lens-shaped, lucid interval; subdural = bridging veins, crescent; subarachnoid = berry aneurysm.
V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 rotundum, V3 ovale, MMA spinosum.
Jugular foramen: IX, X, XI, IJV; XII has its own canal.
Cavernous sinus: ICA and VI inside; III, IV, V1, V2 in the lateral wall; VI palsy first in thrombosis.
Petrosal sinuses drain the cavernous sinus (superior to transverse/sigmoid, inferior to IJV).
Anterior fontanelle closes about 18 months, posterior 2–3 months.
Tongue deviates toward a XII lesion; uvula away from an X lesion.
Stroke (UMN) spares the forehead; Bell palsy (LMN) does not.
CN III palsy: full ptosis, dilated pupil, down and out (PCom aneurysm).
Pituitary adenoma at the chiasm = bitemporal hemianopia.
Corneal reflex: V1 in, VII out; gag: IX in, X out.
hn-face: Blow-out fracture: floor most often; trapped inferior rectus (can't look up), numb cheek (infraorbital n.).
LR6 SO4, the rest III; SO is tested looking down and in.
Near vision: ciliary muscle contracts, zonules relax, lens rounds (III via ciliary ganglion).
Aqueous: ciliary processes → posterior → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm.
Facial nerve branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical.
VII closes the eye; III opens it.
Block too far back into the parotid = temporary facial palsy.
Danger triangle: angular vein → ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus.
Scalp danger zone = loose connective tissue (emissary veins).
Tears: VII → greater petrosal → pterygopalatine ganglion → V2 → V1 → gland; drain to the inferior meatus.
Parotid: facial nerve (superficial), retromandibular vein, ECA (deep); duct opposite maxillary 2nd molar.
Parotid secretion: IX → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal; Frey = gustatory sweating.
hn-itf: Lateral pterygoid = only muscle of mastication that opens and protrudes; superior head to the disc.
Temporalis inserts on the coronoid; posterior fibers retract.
V3 lesion: jaw deviates toward the lesion on opening.
V3 anterior division is motor except the buccal nerve; posterior division is sensory except the nerve to the mylohyoid.
Chorda tympani leaves via the petrotympanic fissure and joins the lingual nerve.
IANB: pterygomandibular space (ramus lateral, medial pterygoid medial); sphenomandibular ligament to the lingula.
IANB misses the buccal nerve; too far back = facial palsy; medial pterygoid trauma = trismus.
PSA block too deep = pterygoid plexus hematoma.
Maxillary a.: 1st part MMA + inferior alveolar; 3rd part PSA, infraorbital, descending palatine, sphenopalatine.
Pterygoid plexus → cavernous sinus via emissary veins through the foramen ovale.
TMJ: fibrocartilage surfaces; hinge in the lower compartment, glide in the upper.
TMJ dislocation is anterior, in front of the articular eminence; TMJ pain refers to the ear (auriculotemporal).
hn-phx: Arch nerves: 1 V, 2 VII, 3 IX, 4 X (superior laryngeal), 6 X (recurrent laryngeal).
Arch 1: malleus, incus, chewing muscles, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, both tensors; arch 2: stapes, styloid, facial muscles, stapedius.
Pouch 3: inferior parathyroid + thymus; pouch 4: superior parathyroid + C cells.
Groove 1 = external acoustic meatus; membrane 1 = tympanic membrane; cervical sinus → lateral cervical cyst at the SCM.
Cleft lip: maxillary prominence + intermaxillary segment; cleft palate: palatine shelves.
Thyroglossal duct cyst: midline, rises with tongue protrusion.
Pharynx: all X except stylopharyngeus (IX); plexus on the middle constrictor.
Gag: IX in, X out; piriform recess fish bone hits the internal laryngeal nerve.
Posterior cricoarytenoid = only abductor; cricothyroid = external laryngeal (pitch).
Cricothyrotomy through the median cricothyroid ligament; cricoid = only complete ring.
Stapedius (VII) lost = hyperacusis; tensor tympani is V3.
Tegmen tympani roof: infection → middle cranial fossa; children's short flat auditory tube → otitis media.
hn-oral: PPF: rotundum (middle cranial fossa), pterygomaxillary fissure (ITF), inferior orbital fissure (orbit), sphenopalatine foramen (nose), palatine canals (palate).
Only parasympathetic fibers (greater petrosal) synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Sinuses drain to the middle meatus except sphenoid (sphenoethmoidal recess) and posterior ethmoid (superior meatus); nasolacrimal duct to the inferior meatus.
Maxillary sinus ostium is high on the medial wall; molar roots lie under its floor (oroantral communication).
Kiesselbach area = anterior nosebleeds; sphenopalatine a. = posterior nosebleeds.
Greater palatine n.: palate molars to canine; nasopalatine n.: behind the incisors (incisive foramen).
Soft palate all X except tensor veli palatini (V3); tongue all XII except palatoglossus (X).
Tongue: front 2/3 V3 + chorda tympani (VII); back 1/3 IX.
Filiform papillae have no taste buds; vallate papillae sit in front of the sulcus terminalis.
Submandibular gland: most resting saliva and most stones; duct opens at the sublingual caruncle.
Tongue tip and mandibular incisors → submental nodes; most teeth → submandibular nodes.
Apex above the mylohyoid line → sublingual space; below (2nd, 3rd molars) → submandibular space; bilateral = Ludwig angina.
da-numbering: FDI quadrants 1 UR, 2 UL, 3 LL, 4 LR (primary 5–8); #8 = 11, #19 = 36, #30 = 46, A = 55, M = 73
Universal primary: A = max right second molar, J = max left second molar, K = mand left second molar, T = mand right second molar
Succedaneous = incisors, canines, premolars; permanent molars are not
Primary order: central, lateral, first molar, canine, second molar (mandibular first); all in by about 2–2½ years
Permanent order: max 6-1-2-4-5-3-7-8, mand 6-1-2-3-4-5-7-8; max canine last anterior (impaction)
First succedaneous tooth: mandibular central incisor (6–7 years)
Primary teeth start calcifying in utero (4–6 months); permanent first molar at birth
Permanent root done 2–3 years after eruption; primary roots done by about 3 years
Primary: thin enamel, large pulps and high MB horns, cervical constriction and ridges, flared molar roots
Primary max central: wider than tall; primary max canine: mesial cusp ridge longer; primary mand first molar: transverse ridge MB to ML
Primary second molars resemble the permanent first molars of the same arch
da-anterior: Facial height of contour: cervical third on every tooth; lingual: cervical third anterior, middle third posterior
Overcontour: food skips the gingiva, plaque collects; undercontour: food packs into the sulcus
Distal contact more cervical than mesial, except mandibular central (level), mandibular PM1 and primary maxillary canine (mesial lower)
Lingual embrasures larger than facial; CEJ curve deepest on the mesial of the central incisors
Maxillary central: sharp MI angle, rounded DI; lateral: centered cingulum, lingual pit, palatogingival groove
Mandibular central: smallest tooth, symmetric, occludes with one tooth; lateral: distolingual twist, distal cingulum
Maxillary canine: longest tooth and root, labial and lingual ridges, mesial cusp ridge shorter
Mandibular canine: longest crown, distal ridge about 2× mesial, straight mesial outline, may have a bifid root
Centered cingulum: maxillary lateral, maxillary canine, mandibular central; slightly distal: maxillary central, mandibular lateral and canine
da-posterior: Maxillary PM1: two roots, mesial crown concavity, mesial marginal ridge groove, lingual cusp mesial of center
Mandibular PM1: canine-like, tiny lingual cusp, mesiolingual groove, mesial marginal ridge more cervical than distal (only posterior tooth)
Mandibular PM2: Y (three cusps, central pit) most common; two-cusp H more common than U; no mesial root depression
Maxillary M1 cusps: ML > MB > DB > DL, Carabelli on ML; oblique ridge DB to ML; wider lingually than buccally
Maxillary molar roots: palatal > MB > DB; MB2 makes 4 canals; mesial furcation most coronal, distal most apical
Mandibular M1: 5 cusps, 2 buccal grooves, D cusp smallest, ML tallest; M2: 4 cusps, + grooves
Mandibular molars: mesial root broader and curved with 2 canals; distal root straighter
Root trunks lengthen and roots converge from first to third molar; third molars most variable and most often missing
Centric cusps: maxillary lingual, mandibular buccal
da-anomalies: Gemination: normal count; fusion (dentin): one short; concrescence: cementum only
Mesiodens: most common supernumerary, between the maxillary centrals (diastema, blocked eruption)
Most often missing: third molars (maxillary more than mandibular)
Amelogenesis imperfecta: enamel only, normal pulps; dentinogenesis imperfecta: blue-gray, obliterated pulps; both hereditary, both dentitions
Turner tooth: one hypoplastic permanent tooth after infection or trauma to the primary tooth
Tetracycline: gray-brown dentin bands; fluorosis: mottled but caries-resistant
Dens in dente and talon cusp: maxillary lateral (anterior cingulum area); taurodontism: tall pulp chamber
Enamel pearl at a furcation: no attachment, localized pocket; dilaceration: bend of 90° or more
Erosion from vomiting: lingual of maxillary anteriors; abfraction: V-shaped cervical; abrasion: rounded
Tooth ID: class by cusps, arch by roots and tilt, then mesial landmark, then side
da-occlusion: Class I: maxillary M1 MB cusp over mandibular M1 buccal groove; maxillary canine between mandibular canine and PM1
Class II: mandible distal; div 1 proclined incisors + overjet; div 2 retroclined centrals + deep bite. Class III: mandible mesial
Centric cusps: maxillary lingual + mandibular buccal (1/3 in, hold VDO); non-centric 1/6 in, protect cheek and tongue
CR: condyles anterosuperior on thin avascular disc, teeth irrelevant; MIP: best fit of teeth; CO: contact at CR; ~90% slide ~1 mm
Optimal: even posterior contacts in CR, axial loads, immediate disclusion in excursions, posterior heavier when upright
Canine guidance: long roots, dense bone, fewer elevators fire; group function: canine + premolars (± MB of M1)
Nonworking contacts are the most damaging interference; balanced occlusion is for dentures
Taller cusps: steep eminence, deep overbite; shorter: overjet, acute Spee, plane ∥ condylar guidance, side shift
Greater intercondylar distance narrows the laterotrusive-mediotrusive angle (the only decrease)
Freeway space 2–4 mm; closest speaking space 1–2 mm; condylar guidance fixed, anterior guidance variable
da-tmj: TMJ: ginglymoarthrodial, compound; fibrous CT surfaces; disc center avascular and non-innervated, posterior band thickest
Superior retrodiscal lamina elastic (pulls the disc back); inferior lamina collagen (limits disc rotation)
Lower compartment = rotation; upper compartment = translation
TM ligament outer oblique limits rotational opening; inner horizontal limits posterior movement; stylomandibular limits protrusion
Moving right: right temporalis + masseter, left lateral + medial pterygoids
Rotation to 20–25 mm, maximum opening 40–60 mm; orbiting condyle goes forward, down and medial
Arcon = condyle on the lower member; facebow mounts the maxillary cast; protrusive record sets condylar inclination
CR mount can find MIP; MIP mount can't find CR
TMD: muscles most common; 5 factors; high crown → protective co-contraction; bruxism central; reversible care first
Occlusal trauma doesn't cause periodontitis or attachment loss; reversible; tooth 28 µm vs implant 2–3 µm
Miller 1 barely, 2 ≤1 mm, 3 >1 mm or depressible; abrasion: toothpaste matters more than the brush
f1-biomol: Noncovalent strength: ionic > hydrogen bond > van der Waals; hydrogen bonds need N, O or F.
Blood pH 7.35–7.45; a buffer works best at pH = pKa; bicarbonate is the main blood buffer: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− (carbonic anhydrase).
Side-chain pKa: Asp 3.9, Glu 4.3, His 6.0 (the body-pH buffer), Cys 8.3, Lys 10.5, Arg 12.5.
Glycine is achiral; proteins use L amino acids; proline breaks α-helices (3.6 residues per turn).
Collagen: Gly-X-Y; type I is over 90% (bone, dentin, PDL); II cartilage, III reticular, IV basement membrane.
Vitamin C → prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in the RER; no vitamin C = scurvy (bleeding gums, poor healing).
Outside the cell: procollagen peptidases cut propeptides; lysyl oxidase (copper) cross-links.
Osteogenesis imperfecta: type I collagen (COL1A1, COL1A2); fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta.
Hemoglobin: T (deoxy) to R (oxy), cooperative, sigmoidal; myoglobin: monomer, hyperbolic.
Right shift: ↑ H+, CO2, 2,3-BPG, temperature. Left shift: fetal Hb (α2γ2), CO, cold.
Glucose/galactose are C-4 epimers; glucose/mannose C-2; α/β are anomers. Sucrose feeds S. mutans glucans.
Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids by ester bonds; A–T 2 hydrogen bonds, G–C 3; purines → uric acid.
Globular protein classes: all α, all β, α/β (mixed) and α+β (separate domains). Folds rest on many hydrogen bonds and a hydrophobic core.
Quaternary structure: stability (lower surface-to-volume), genetic economy, shared catalytic sites, cooperativity; globular subunits held noncovalently.
Collagen chain: left-handed helix, 3.3 residues/turn; triple helix right-handed, 300 nm × 1.4 nm; 68 nm banding with 40 nm hole zones.
Heme: His F8 is the fifth ligand, O2 the sixth. P50 of HbA 26 mmHg (higher P50 = lower affinity). HbF: Ser for His 143 → less 2,3-BPG.
Sucrose (α1→β2) is nonreducing; lactose β-1,4; maltose α-1,4; cellulose β-1,4; glycogen α-1,4 with α-1,6 branches.
N-glycans: Asn in Asn-X-Ser/Thr, dolichol precursor, ER then Golgi. O-glycans: Ser/Thr, one sugar at a time, mostly Golgi. ABO: A adds GalNAc, B galactose, O inactive.
RNA: ribose (2′-OH, easily hydrolyzed), uracil, usually one strand. Nucleosome: DNA around 8 histones (4 kinds × 2) + H1.
f1-cells: Address tags: signal peptide → RER; mannose-6-phosphate → lysosome; ubiquitin → proteasome; NLS → nucleus.
Lysosome pH 4.5–5.0; peroxisome catalase breaks H2O2; mitochondria have their own (maternal) DNA.
Microtubules: spindle, cilia, flagella. Actin: microvilli, movement. Intermediate filaments: tensile strength.
Apoptosis = caspases, non-inflammatory; necrosis is inflammatory.
Reflection coefficient: 0 = freely permeable (no osmotic effect), 1 = impermeant (full effect).
Hypotonic → cell swells; hypertonic → cell shrinks. Particles per molecule: NaCl 2, MgCl2 3, glucose 1. Plasma about 290 mOsm/L.
Na+/K+ ATPase: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in (primary active). SGLT = cotransport; Na+/Ca2+ exchanger = countertransport.
Nernst: 60 mV per tenfold gradient (z = 1) at 37 °C; resting potential (−70 mV) sits near E(K+) because K+ leak dominates; the pump adds only a few mV.
Upstroke = voltage-gated Na+ in; repolarization = Na+ inactivation + K+ out; absolute refractory = Na+ inactivated.
Local anesthetics block Na+ channels from inside; acidic infected tissue weakens them. Tetrodotoxin blocks Na+ channels from outside; TEA blocks K+ channels (wide action potential).
EPSP: glutamate, Na+ in. IPSP: GABA or glycine, Cl− in. Ca2+ entry triggers transmitter release.
Botulinum cleaves SNAP-25 (no ACh release); myasthenia gravis = antibodies against the ACh receptor (release normal), helped by AChE inhibitors; cocaine and SSRIs block reuptake.
Hyperkalemia depolarizes (mild: nearer threshold; enough: Na+ channels locked inactivated, weakness). Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes (less excitable). Normal K+ 3.5–5.0 mmol/L.
Na+ channel: activation (m) gate closed at rest, opens fast; inactivation (h) gate open at rest, closes slowly. Refractoriness keeps conduction one-way.
Myelin: oligodendrocytes (CNS, many axons) and Schwann cells (PNS, one segment of one axon); Na+ channels cluster at the nodes.
Smooth ER: lipids, drug detoxification, Ca2+ store. Filament width: microtubules 24 nm > intermediate 10 nm > actin 7 nm.
Metabotropic receptors always act through a G protein (slower); ionotropic receptors are channels (fast). Spatial summation = many synapses at once; temporal = one synapse in quick succession.
f1-molbio: Replication is semiconservative, in S phase; new DNA always grows 5′ → 3′ on a primer's 3′-OH.
Bacteria: primase → Pol III copies → Pol I removes primers → ligase seals; gyrase relieves supercoils.
Eukaryotes: many origins, Pol α/δ/ε, PCNA clamp; telomerase (reverse transcriptase) adds TTAGGG.
σ reads −35 TTGACA and −10 TATAAT; rifampin binds β; rho-dependent or hairpin + U-run termination.
Lac operon fully on only with lactose present and glucose absent (repressor off, CAP–cAMP on).
Pol I large rRNA, Pol II mRNA (α-amanitin), Pol III tRNA and 5S; TFIID's TBP binds the TATA box.
Cap (5′–5′), splicing (GU...AG, lariat), poly(A) tail (no template); acetylation on, CpG methylation off.
AUG start; UAA, UAG, UGA stop; wobble at codon base 3; peptidyl transferase is rRNA (a ribozyme).
AD every generation; AR skips (unaffected sib 2/3 carrier); XLR males via carrier mothers, no father-to-son.

Sickle cell = missense Glu → Val (a transversion); frameshift = indel not a multiple of 3 (acridine dyes); repeats with anticipation: Huntington (CAG), fragile X, Friedreich ataxia, myotonic dystrophy (CTG).
Oncogenes one hit (HER2, RAS, BCR-ABL); tumor suppressors two hits (RB, p53, APC); HPV E6 → p53, E7 → RB.
Chargaff: A = T and G = C (30% A → 30% T, 20% G, 20% C); DNA polymerase needs a primer, proofreads 3′ → 5′, errs about 1 in 10 million.
lacI mutant (no repressor) = constitutive lac expression; RNA polymerase errs about 1 in 10,000 bases.
Poly(A) about 200–250 A's; U1 at the 5′ splice site, U2 at the branch point; apoB-48 = C → U edit to a UAA stop.
Test cross: dominant-trait individual × homozygous recessive; any recessive offspring = heterozygous.
Ames test: histidine-requiring Salmonella grow back only if a chemical mutates them; aflatoxin (peanut mold), nitrosamines (smoke).
Teeth: amelogenesis imperfecta (enamel), dentinogenesis imperfecta (dentin; blue-gray or brown, translucent), ectodermal dysplasia (missing or pointed teeth).
FAP = APC; Lynch = mismatch repair; Li-Fraumeni = TP53; HER2 → trastuzumab; BCR-ABL t(9;22) → imatinib.
f1-enzhorm: Endocrine = blood (GH, insulin); paracrine = neighbors (Leydig testosterone); autocrine = self (estradiol).
Peptides: preprohormone, granules, surface receptors, not oral. Steroids: cholesterol, carriers, nuclear receptors, oral.
Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA (cAMP frees catalytic subunits); Gq → PLC → IP3 (Ca2+) + DAG (PKC).
Insulin: β cells, Ca2+-triggered release, receptor tyrosine kinase, GLUT4 to muscle and fat membranes.
Cholesterol → pregnenolone (mitochondria, P450 side-chain cleavage, NADPH + O2) is the rate-limiting steroid step; ACTH drives adrenal cortisol and androgen synthesis.
Transcortin carries about 75% of cortisol; SHBG carries testosterone and estradiol.
Cushing = excess cortisol (most often iatrogenic); Conn = excess aldosterone (HTN, low K+; adenoma); Addison = low both (usually autoimmune), high ACTH, oral pigmentation.
PTH and calcitriol raise Ca2+; calcitonin lowers it (inhibits osteoclasts).
Catabolic: oxidative, exergonic, NAD+. Anabolic: reductive, endergonic, NADPH. Brain and RBCs: glucose.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG < 0 spontaneous, 0 at equilibrium; says nothing about rate. Enzymes don't change ΔG.
Km = [S] at ½Vmax (low Km = tight binding); kcat = Vmax/[E]; kcat/Km = efficiency (diffusion-limited).
Competitive (malonate at SDH, methotrexate): Km ↑, Vmax same (cross on y). Noncompetitive: Vmax ↓, Km same (cross on x). Uncompetitive (lithium): both ↓, parallel. Penicillin: irreversible (suicide).
Enzyme traits: catalytic power, specificity (the active site) and regulation. Cofactor = metal ion; coenzyme = vitamin-derived; protein alone = apoenzyme, with its cofactor = holoenzyme.
ΔG°′ goes with the equilibrium constant (how far); ΔG‡ with the rate constant (how fast). Enzymes lower only ΔG‡; induced fit (hexokinase) beats lock and key.
Bisubstrate: sequential (ordered or random, creatine kinase) lines cross left of the 1/v axis; ping-pong (aminotransferases) lines are parallel.
ATP → ADP + Pi: about −30.5 kJ/mol (−7.3 kcal/mol), Mg2+-bound; powers mechanical, transport and chemical work; about 50 g recycled about 1,300 times a day.
f1-carbmet: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose; the rate-limiting enzyme is PFK-1 (on: AMP, fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, Pi; off: ATP, citrate, H+).
Red cells end glycolysis at lactate (lactate dehydrogenase) to regenerate NAD+; the lactate goes to the liver (Cori cycle).
PDH works in the mitochondrial matrix with five coenzymes: thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD+. It is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA can't make glucose.

Citric acid cycle per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, 2 CO2. Rate-limiting: isocitrate dehydrogenase (on: ADP, NAD+; off: ATP, NADH); citrate synthase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are slowed by NADH and succinyl-CoA.
Protons pumped per electron pair: Complex I 4, II 0, III 4, IV 2. NADH ≈ 2.5 ATP, FADH2 ≈ 1.5 ATP.
About 32 ATP per glucose with the malate-aspartate shuttle, 30 with the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle.
Cyanide, carbon monoxide and azide block Complex IV; rotenone Complex I; antimycin A Complex III; oligomycin ATP synthase.
Uncouplers (DNP, aspirin overdose, brown fat's thermogenin): oxygen use up, ATP down, heat out.
Glucagon and epinephrine → cAMP → phosphorylase on, glycogen synthase off; insulin reverses both.

Gluconeogenesis bypasses: pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondria, biotin, activated by acetyl-CoA) and PEP carboxykinase (GTP); fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase; glucose 6-phosphatase (liver and kidney, never muscle).
No net glucose from even-chain fatty acids or the ketogenic amino acids leucine and lysine.
PDH off: acetyl-CoA, NADH and ATP activate PDH kinase, which phosphorylates E1; a phosphatase turns it back on.
Liver glycogen: up to 10% of the liver's weight, lasts 12–24 h of fasting; muscle holds about twice as much in total but can't release glucose.
No glucose 6-phosphatase (or its ER translocase) = von Gierke disease: glycogen fills the liver, with fasting hypoglycemia.
Cori cycle: costs energy (6 ATP in the liver for 2 in the tissue), needs no mitochondria. Alanine cycle: needs mitochondria, adds urea.
f1-innate: Neutrophils are the most abundant blood leukocyte, arrive first in acute bacterial infection and make pus.
Mast cells live in tissue; basophils circulate. Eosinophils fight helminths with major basic protein.
NK cells are lymphoid by lineage, innate by function: they kill cells missing MHC I and IgG-coated cells (CD16, ADCC).
Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow and thymus. Secondary: lymph nodes, spleen (filters blood), MALT (tonsils, Peyer's patches).
TLR4 senses LPS; NLR inflammasomes → caspase-1 → IL-1β and IL-18 (pyroptosis); RIG-I-like receptors sense cytosolic viral dsRNA → NF-κB and IRFs (type I interferon).
Respiratory burst: NADPH oxidase → superoxide → hydrogen peroxide → hypochlorite (myeloperoxidase). CGD: infections with catalase-positive organisms.

C3 is the key: all complement pathways meet at C3 (the alternative usually acts first, since C3 is in every tissue). C3b opsonizes; C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins; C5a draws neutrophils; C5b–C9 lyses.
C1 inhibitor deficiency = hereditary angioedema (low C4, bradykinin, swelling after dental work). C5–C9 deficiency = recurrent Neisseria.

Extravasation: selectins bind mucin-like CAMs (rolling) → chemokines → integrins bind Ig-superfamily CAMs (LFA-1 on neutrophils binds ICAM-1; Mac-1 on monocytes) → diapedesis → chemotaxis. Cells arrive in order: neutrophils, monocytes, then basophils, eosinophils, lymphocytes.
Apoptosis is silent (DAMPs sequestered); necrosis, necroptosis (apoptosis blocked), pyroptosis and NETosis (neutrophils only) release DAMPs and inflame.
IL-6 makes the liver produce CRP and the other acute phase proteins; IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α cause fever.
PRRs: about 100 invariant, germline receptors. CLRs and TLRs drive phagocytosis; TLRs, NLRs and RLRs drive NF-κB, the key to proinflammatory cytokines.
Early monocytes become M1 (inflammatory) macrophages; later ones become M2 (resolution and repair). Unresolved acute inflammation becomes chronic.
Prostaglandins and leukotrienes are lipid mediators made from arachidonic acid in membrane phospholipids; NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase.
Chemical barriers: defensins (α, β; bacteria and enveloped viruses), lysozyme (cuts peptidoglycan; saliva, tears), α2-macroglobulin (blocks microbial proteases).
Cytokines tell cells what to do, chemokines where to go. Pleiotropy: one cytokine, many effects; redundancy: many cytokines, one effect.
f1-adaptive: IgM: pentamer, first antibody, best complement activator. IgG: most abundant in serum, secondary response, crosses the placenta (FcRn).
Secretory IgA is a dimer with a J chain and secretory component (left from the poly-Ig receptor); it guards saliva, tears, milk and gut.
IgE sits on mast cells (allergy, helminths); IgD sits on naive B cells with IgM.
Heavy chains join V + D + J; light chains V + J only. RAG1 and RAG2 cut; TdT adds random nucleotides. A B cell's secreted antibody has the same specificity as its BCR.
Class switching needs CD40–CD40L, cytokines and AID; a CD40L defect gives hyper-IgM syndrome.
MHC I: all nucleated cells, cytosolic peptides loaded in the ER after TAP, read by CD8. MHC II: APCs, engulfed peptides (invariant chain, CLIP, HLA-DM), read by CD4.
T-cell activation: signal 1 TCR with peptide–MHC, signal 2 B7–CD28, signal 3 IL-2. No signal 2 = anergy.
Th1 (IL-12) makes IFN-γ; Th2 (IL-4) makes IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; Th17 (TGF-β, IL-6, IL-23) makes IL-17; Tregs (IL-2, TGF-β) need FoxP3 and make TGF-β and IL-10; Tfh make IL-21 and IL-6.
Type I interferons from infected cells and plasmacytoid DCs make neighbors antiviral and activate NK cells, which kill "missing self".
Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, yellow fever) are not given to immunocompromised patients or in pregnancy.
Hepatitis B vaccine is recombinant surface antigen; anti-HBs of 10 mIU/mL or more after the series means protected.
Passive immunity is immediate and leaves no memory. Conjugate vaccines (Hib, pneumococcal) give T-cell help against polysaccharides.
RNA splicing, not DNA recombination, lets a naive B cell show IgM and IgD together and decides membrane-bound or secreted antibody.

CD8 priming needs TCR with peptide–MHC I, costimulation and CD4 help; killing in the tissue needs only TCR with peptide–MHC I. NK cells read the level of MHC I, not the peptide.

f1-hyper: Positive selection (thymic cortex): weak binding of self-MHC survives, none means death by neglect; class I binders become CD8, class II binders CD4.

B cells: the pre-BCR uses a surrogate light chain; receptor editing swaps only the light chain; mature naive B cells carry IgM and IgD by RNA splicing, not DNA recombination.
Peripheral tolerance: naive cells kept out of tissues, anergy (no costimulation), activation-induced cell death (Fas–FasL), Tregs (CD4+CD25+FoxP3+; IL-10, TGF-β, soaking up IL-2). FOXP3 loss = IPEX.

Type I: IgE on mast cells; immediate phase within 30 minutes (histamine), late phase 4+ hours (eosinophils, IL-5, leukotrienes). IgE's real job: helminths. Intramuscular epinephrine first.
Type II: antibody, mostly IgG, against cells or matrix (transfusion reaction, Rh disease, drug hemolytic anemia, pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, Graves). IgG crosses the placenta, IgM does not.
Type III: small immune complexes with soluble antigen, poorly cleared (SLE with anti-dsDNA, serum sickness, Arthus reaction at 4–8 hours).
Type IV: T cells, 24–72 hours after re-exposure, sensitization at least 7 days (nickel, poison ivy, glove accelerators, tuberculin test, granulomas, celiac disease, type 1 diabetes).
Penicillin can cause all four types: its reactive bond binds host proteins and makes neoantigens.

Alkaline urine (sodium bicarbonate) traps a weak acid such as aspirin; acid urine traps a weak base such as amphetamine.

Loading dose = Vd × target concentration; maintenance rate = clearance × target concentration.

Zero-order (a constant amount per hour): ethanol, phenytoin, high-dose aspirin.
CYP inhibitors: clarithromycin, erythromycin, azoles (ketoconazole, fluconazole), ritonavir, grapefruit. Inducers: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort, smoking.

IND before the first human dose. Phase I: 20–100 healthy volunteers, safety. Phase II: 100–500 patients, efficacy. Phase III: 1,000–5,000 patients, then the NDA. Phase IV: rare harms after approval.
Affinity (1/KD) is shared by full agonists, partial agonists and antagonists; only agonists have intrinsic activity (a partial agonist: high affinity, low intrinsic activity).
Therapeutic window: the plasma levels between the MEC and the MTC.
Synergism: alcohol with a benzodiazepine (more than the sum). Additive: oxycodone with acetaminophen.
Vd: 3–5 L plasma, 12–14 L extracellular fluid, about 42 L total body water, far more in tissues (amiodarone, tricyclics).
AUC: total exposure. Cmax: the peak; Tmax: its time; Cmin: the trough at the end of the interval.
After stopping, each half-life halves the level: falling to a quarter takes two half-lives. CL = ke × Vd.
Renal clearance above the GFR (about 120 mL/min) means tubular secretion; below it, reabsorption.
Metabolism makes drugs more polar: it inactivates, activates a prodrug (codeine), leaves an active metabolite (diazepam → oxazepam) or makes a toxin (NAPQI).
Polymorphic: CYP2D6 (codeine), CYP2C9 (warfarin), CYP2C19 (omeprazole), N-acetyltransferase. P-gp pumps drugs out of cells.

Pilocarpine and cevimeline (M3 agonists) bring back saliva while some gland tissue remains.

Nonselective β-blocker plus epinephrine: hypertension with reflex bradycardia; keep epinephrine to about 0.04 mg.
α1 blockers (-osin) cause orthostatic hypotension: bring the chair up slowly.

Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, so ACh isn't released.
f2-painrx: Steroids block phospholipase A2, NSAIDs block COX, zileuton blocks 5-lipoxygenase.

Aminoglycosides: kidney and ear damage; no anaerobic coverage.
Metronidazole: anaerobes and protozoa; no alcohol; raises the INR.

cr-bp: Carotid sinus → CN IX; aortic arch → CN X; low pressure → less firing → more sympathetic outflow.
Vasovagal syncope, the most common dental emergency: HR and BP both fall; lay the patient flat, legs up.
Renin comes from juxtaglomerular cells; ACE in the lungs makes angiotensin II; aldosterone keeps Na+ and loses K+.
ANP from stretched atria and BNP from the ventricles cause Na+ and water loss.
Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing (raised intracranial pressure).
Septic shock: warm skin, high cardiac output, low SVR; hypovolemic and cardiogenic: cold skin, high SVR.
Hypertension: stage 1 is 130–139/80–89, stage 2 is 140/90 or higher.
Inferior MI (II, III, aVF) = right coronary artery; anterior (V1–V4) = LAD.
Free wall rupture after an MI: 3–10 days, when the infarct is softest. Elective dental care waits: 6 months on the slides, about 30 days for a stable patient in newer guidance.
Endocarditis after dental care: viridans streptococci; prophylaxis is amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 minutes before, for high-risk patients only.
BP of 180/110 or higher: defer elective dental care and refer.
Autoregulation (the myogenic response plus metabolites) is best in the kidney, heart and brain; NO dilates, endothelin-1 constricts; low O2 dilates every bed but the lungs.
Shock: MAP under about 70 with a fast pulse, cold skin, little urine, confusion, lactate over 2 mmol/L; distributive is the most prevalent type; epinephrine first for anaphylaxis.
HFrEF: EF under 40%, dilated (ischemia); HFpEF: EF 50% or more, thick and stiff (hypertension); most right-sided failure comes from left-sided.
Giant cell arteritis (over 50, more women): headache, tender temporal artery, jaw pain on chewing; refer the same day (vision loss).
cr-cvdrugs: Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine most) cause gingival overgrowth in about 6–34%: slower collagen breakdown (less MMP activity) and more fibroblasts.
ACE inhibitors: dry cough and angioedema from bradykinin; ARBs rarely.
Nonselective β-blocker + epinephrine → hypertension with a reflex slow heart.
Cardiac epinephrine limit 0.04 mg ≈ two cartridges of 1:100,000 (0.018 mg each); healthy adult 0.2 mg.
Thiazides lower Na+, K+ and Mg2+ and raise calcium, glucose and uric acid; loops lower K+, Mg2+ and Na+, send calcium into the urine (serum calcium usually normal) and are ototoxic.
Digoxin blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase; low K+ makes it toxic (nausea, yellow halos).
Mortality-lowering heart failure drugs: ACE inhibitor/ARB or sacubitril–valsartan, select β-blocker, aldosterone antagonist, SGLT2 inhibitor.
Amiodarone (class III): lung fibrosis, thyroid changes, liver injury, blue-gray skin, corneal deposits, optic neuropathy.
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; clarithromycin and erythromycin raise myopathy risk.
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg under the tongue every 5 minutes, up to three doses; never after sildenafil or tadalafil.
Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar vasodilator (reflex tachycardia, lupus-like syndrome), not a nitrate.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs: high K+, kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis, no use in pregnancy; NSAIDs add to both risks.
Sacubitril–valsartan: contraindicated in pregnancy and after angioedema from an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
Class I widens the QRS most, class III lengthens the QT most; classes II and IV for rate control, I and III for rhythm control.
PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL the most; bile acid sequestrants bind other drugs (give those 1–2 h before or 4 h after).
cr-blood: vWF links platelet GpIb to collagen; GpIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen; vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.
Tissue factor with factor VII starts clotting; factors V and VIII are cofactors.
Vitamin K–dependent: II, VII, IX, X, proteins C and S; factor VII has the shortest half-life.
PT/INR: warfarin, liver disease, factor VII. aPTT: heparin, hemophilia A, B and C (VIII, IX, XI); factor XII lack doesn't bleed.
Extractions on warfarin usually go ahead with an INR of 3.5 or less and local measures.
Reversal: warfarin, vitamin K or PCC; heparin, protamine; dabigatran, idarucizumab; -xabans, andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks COX-1 for the 7–10 day life of the platelet.
Tranexamic acid blocks fibrinolysis; alteplase activates plasminogen.
Sickle cell: valine for glutamic acid at β6; sickle trait is the most common hemoglobinopathy in the US; HbC (lysine) is mild, with target cells.
α-thalassemia: three genes lost = HbH disease; four = Hb Barts and hydrops.
Iron deficiency is microcytic, low ferritin the most sensitive test (ferrous sulfate); B12 and folate are macrocytic; only B12 fixes the nerves.
Epoetin for the anemia of kidney disease; filgrastim for neutropenia (bone pain).
Bernard–Soulier: no GpIb, giant platelets, no ristocetin response; Glanzmann: no GpIIb/IIIa, normal-sized platelets.
Factor V Leiden (resists activated protein C), prothrombin G20210A and a lack of protein C, S or antithrombin cause clots, not bleeding.
HIT: days 5–10, antibodies to heparin–platelet factor 4; platelets fall while clots form; stop heparin, give bivalirudin.
Ticagrelor is cleared by CYP3A4: never with clarithromycin. Avoid NSAIDs with any anticoagulant or antiplatelet.
B12 needs acid, intrinsic factor and the ileum; PPIs, H2 blockers, metformin and nitrous oxide lower it.
cr-resp: Aspirated objects usually go down the right main bronchus.
The intercostal bundle runs under each rib (vein, artery, nerve), so needles go over the top of a rib.
Type II pneumocytes make surfactant (DPPC); they mature at about 35 weeks, so earlier babies get neonatal RDS.
Spirometry can't measure RV, FRC or TLC.
Alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate; doubling ventilation halves PaCO2.
V/Q is highest at the apex and lowest at the base; a shunt barely responds to 100% O2.
Right shift: CO2, acid, 2,3-BPG, exercise, heat. Carbon monoxide shifts left.
Central chemoreceptors sense H+ from CO2; peripheral ones sense PO2 below about 60 mmHg.
The medulla (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups) sets the breathing rhythm; the pons only fine-tunes it.
Obstructive: FEV1/FVC under 0.7, high TLC. Restrictive: normal or high ratio, low TLC.
Inhaled steroids cause oral candidiasis: spacer, rinse and spit.
Tetracyclines stain developing teeth; fluoroquinolones cause tendon rupture.
Alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) − PaCO2 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 150 − 50 = 100 mmHg.
V/Q of 0 (blocked airway): alveolar gas = mixed venous (PO2 40, PCO2 45). V/Q near infinity (embolus): alveolar gas = inspired air (PO2 about 150, PCO2 0).
Zone 1 (alveolar > arterial pressure): no flow, only with hemorrhage or positive-pressure breathing; zone 3, at the base, has the most. Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at FRC.
Visceral pleura isn't sensitive to sharp pain; costal pleura hurts over the chest wall (intercostal nerves), diaphragmatic pleura in the neck (phrenic, C3–C5).
Chronic CO2 retention: the choroid plexus adds bicarbonate to the CSF, so the central chemoreceptors reset to the higher PaCO2.
Aspirin-sensitive asthma (with nasal polyps, Samter's triad): no aspirin or NSAIDs; use acetaminophen.
Sarcoidosis: noncaseating granulomas, high ACE and calcium; parotid enlargement + uveitis + facial palsy = Heerfordt syndrome.
Strawberry gingivitis + sinusitis + kidney disease = granulomatosis with polyangiitis: biopsy and refer.
COPD in the chair: semi-reclined, no nitrous oxide; tiotropium and ipratropium dry the mouth.
rn-filtration: Kidneys: retroperitoneal, T12–L3, right lower (liver); 20–25% of cardiac output.
GFR about 100–125 mL/min (144–180 L/day); filtration fraction = GFR/RPF ≈ 20%; glomerular Kf about 100 times that of systemic capillaries.
Net filtration (class example): (45 − 10) − 19 = 16 mmHg; oncotic pressure rises to about 35 by the efferent end (net 0).

Efferent constriction (angiotensin II): RPF down, GFR held up. Afferent constriction: both down. ACE inhibitor: GFR down. Ureter stone or high plasma protein: GFR down, RPF unchanged; low plasma protein: GFR up.
Autoregulation 80–200 mmHg: myogenic + tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa → adenosine → afferent constriction).
C = UV/P. Inulin = GFR; PAH ≈ RPF, and RBF = RPF ÷ (1 − Hct); creatinine ≈ GFR (doubling creatinine = halving GFR; muscle mass, creatine and meat raise it).
Clearance ratio: 1 filtered only; above 1 secreted; below 1 reabsorbed or not filtered.
60–40–20: TBW 60%, ICF 40%, ECF 20% (the course: 80% interstitial, 20% plasma; often rounded to 3/4 and 1/4).
Bladder: sympathetic stores (internal sphincter closed); parasympathetic S2–S4 voids (detrusor); pudendal closes external sphincter; the pontine micturition center decides when.
Clearance 0: albumin (not filtered) and glucose (filtered, all reabsorbed). Maximum clearance = RPF (PAH).
ECF: Na+ main cation, Cl− then HCO3− anions; ICF: K+ then Mg2+. Water moves until ICF and ECF osmolarity match.
Active vitamin D = 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, made by renal 1α-hydroxylase (low Ca2+, high PTH, low phosphate); 24,25 is inactive.
rn-tubule: Na+ reabsorbed: PT 65%, loop (TAL) 25%, DCT 5%, collecting duct 4–5%. Water: PT 65%, thin descending limb 10%, collecting duct 5% (water load) to more than 24% (dehydration).
PT: Na+/H+ exchanger + carbonic anhydrase (HCO3−), SGLT2 (glucose), iso-osmotic water; secretes PAH and penicillin.
Glucose: threshold about 200 mg/dL (first spills into the urine), Tm about 350 mg/dL (every carrier saturated), splay between; glycosuria and osmotic diuresis.
Thin descending: water out. Thin ascending: NaCl out, no water. TAL: NKCC2, ROMK, lumen positive, paracellular Ca2+ and Mg2+, diluting segment.
Medullary gradient 300 → 1,200 mOsm/kg with ADH (about 600 without): half NaCl (countercurrent multiplication), half urea (recycling); vasa recta preserve it.
DCT: NCC (thiazides); TRPV5 Ca2+ entry under PTH; thiazides lower urinary Ca2+.
Principal cells: ENaC, ROMK, AQP2 (ADH via V2/cAMP), aldosterone adds channels over hours.
α-intercalated: H+ secretion, K+ reabsorption, AE1; β-intercalated: pendrin HCO3− secretion.
Secondary active transport: apical Na+ cotransporters and exchangers run on the Na+ gradient the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase keeps.
ECF volume expansion lowers proximal reabsorption; contraction raises it. Along the PT: Na+ stays at plasma level, Cl− rises, glucose and HCO3− fall.
Several nephrons drain into one collecting duct (connecting tubules merge at the cortical collecting duct).
rn-balance: ADH: supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei → posterior pituitary; osmoreceptors in OVLT and SFO; ADH at 1–2%, thirst at 2–3%.
Volume (5–10% fall) overrides osmolarity; alcohol suppresses ADH.
SIADH: low Na+, concentrated urine → fluid restriction (acute: furosemide + 3% saline). Central DI → desmopressin. Nephrogenic DI (lithium) → thiazide, amiloride.
RAAS: renin for low afferent pressure, sympathetic β1, low macula densa NaCl (via prostaglandins). ANP from stretched atria opposes it: it inhibits renin, aldosterone, ADH and Na+ reabsorption.
K+: 98% intracellular; 3.5–5.0 mEq/L. Into cells: insulin, β2 agonists, α-blockers, alkalosis, aldosterone. Out: α agonists, β-blockers, acidosis, cell lysis.
K+ secretion up: aldosterone (mostly through ENaC Na+ reabsorption), high K+ diet, alkalosis, high flow (loop, thiazide). Down: acidosis, spironolactone, amiloride, low GFR, NSAIDs in CKD.
Mg2+: TAL about 60% (main site). Ca2+: PT 65%, TAL 20–25%, DCT 5–10%. Phosphate: PT 85%. Loop diuretics lose Ca2+ and Mg2+; thiazides keep Ca2+.
PTH: Ca2+ up, phosphate down, calcitriol up. FGF23: phosphaturia, calcitriol and PTH down. Calcitriol: gut Ca2+ absorption.
Net acid excretion = NH4+ + titratable acid − HCO3−; each H+ excreted adds a new HCO3−.
Metabolic acidosis → hyperventilation; metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) → hypoventilation, lasting until the lost volume is replaced; respiratory disorders → renal compensation over days.
Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3), normal 8–12; DKA, lactate, salicylate, uremia raise it.
ADH: V2 → collecting duct water (aquaporin-2) and inner medullary urea; V1 → arteriolar constriction.
Heart failure edema: Na+ and water in the interstitium, unseen by the baroreceptors; low effective circulating volume → more Na+ retention.
Blood gas arrows: PCO2 and HCO3− opposite to the pH = respiratory; same way as the pH = metabolic.
rn-disease: CKD: abnormal structure or function 3 months or more; diabetes first, hypertension second.
uACR under 30 mg/g normal; picks up damage when eGFR is still above 60.
Function holds until more than 50% of nephrons are lost.
Azotemia = lab (BUN and creatinine up); uremia = clinical illness.
CKD: anemia (low EPO), hypertension, hyperkalemia, acidosis, secondary hyperparathyroidism, platelet dysfunction.
Nephritic: hematuria, hypertension, oliguria (PSGN, IgA, RPGN). Nephrotic: proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia (minimal change, FSGS, membranous, MPGN).
PSGN 1–4 weeks after strep, low C3, humps. IgA: days after infection, most common GN worldwide. RPGN: crescents.
Stones: calcium 75%, struvite 15% (alkaline infected urine, staghorn). Pyelonephritis: E. coli, WBC casts.
ADPKD: PKD1/PKD2, adults, berry aneurysms. Clear cell RCC: VHL 3p. Wilms: children, triphasic.
Deposits: subepithelial (membranous spikes, PSGN humps); subendothelial (MPGN I); mesangial IgA (IgA nephropathy); linear IgG (anti-GBM); none, effaced podocytes (minimal change).
rn-dental: Loop (furosemide): NKCC2, most potent; low K+, Na+ and Mg2+, Ca2+ lost in the urine, ototoxicity; works for hypertension when CrCl is under 30.
Thiazide: NCC; first-line for hypertension; the diuretic most likely to cause hyponatremia; low K+, high Ca2+, glucose, lipids, uric acid; weak when GFR is low.
Spironolactone: hyperkalemia, gynecomastia. Amiloride: ENaC, hyperkalemia.
Acetazolamide: hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Mannitol: osmotic; not in heart failure.
Hemodialysis: treat the day after; never the fistula arm for BP or IVs.
Uremic platelets bleed even with a normal count; plan local hemostasis.
Avoid NSAIDs, tetracycline (not doxycycline), meperidine. Acetaminophen is the analgesic of choice.
Lengthen intervals for amoxicillin, penicillin VK, cephalexin; give after dialysis. Lidocaine, clindamycin, azithromycin, metronidazole: no change.
Oral: ammonia breath, uremic stomatitis (red, sore mouth), xerostomia, metallic taste, pallor, petechiae. Radiograph: lost lamina dura, ground glass, brown tumors.
Transplant: cyclosporine gingival overgrowth; screen for oral cancer; avoid clarithromycin, erythromycin and azoles with cyclosporine or tacrolimus.
Acute kidney injury: no NSAIDs, no high-dose acyclovir, lower renal doses, hydrate, defer elective care.
Diabetic kidney disease (most common): perio, infection, slow healing. Hypertensive or polycystic: steady BP, careful epinephrine.
he-axes: Gs (cAMP up): ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, glucagon, PTH. Gq (IP3, calcium): TRH, GnRH, oxytocin, angiotensin II. Gi: somatostatin, dopamine. Tyrosine kinase: insulin. JAK2: GH, prolactin.
Steroids are made on demand from cholesterol, carried on proteins, and act on intracellular receptors; thyroid hormone also uses a nuclear receptor.
Primary gland failure: target hormone and pituitary hormone move opposite. Secondary (pituitary): same direction.
Posterior pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus (Herring bodies). Dopamine inhibits prolactin.
GH: pulses in deep sleep; GHRH up, somatostatin down; IGF-1 from the liver grows bone; diabetogenic and lipolytic.
Acromegaly: Class III jaw, diastemas, macroglossia; confirm with GH that fails to suppress after glucose.
Prolactinoma = most common functioning adenoma (dopamine agonist). Macroadenoma: bitemporal hemianopsia. Sheehan: no lactation after delivery.
Central DI: dilute urine, high sodium, fixed by desmopressin. SIADH: low sodium, small cell lung cancer.
Cortex: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens): salt, sugar, sex. Medulla: 80% epinephrine (PNMT induced by cortisol).
Addison: ACTH high → oral pigmentation, low sodium, high potassium. Cushing: ACTH high = pituitary or ectopic; ACTH low = adrenal or pills. Conn: renin low.
Fludrocortisone = salt (Addison). Dexamethasone = strong, long, no salt. Taper because the axis is suppressed.
Adrenal crisis: hypotension, confusion, shock after stress or a missed dose → 911, supine, oxygen, 100 mg hydrocortisone IV or IM.
he-thyroid: TPO organifies and couples iodine on thyroglobulin; the hormone is stored in the colloid. The gland releases mostly T4; 5′-deiodinase makes active T3.
Graves: stimulating TSH-receptor IgG, exophthalmos; TSH low, T4 high. Hashimoto: anti-TPO, lymphocytes; TSH high, T4 low.
Hyper: weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, early eruption; limit epinephrine when uncontrolled. Hypo: macroglossia, bradycardia, delayed eruption and healing.
Thyroid storm: fever, pulse 140 or more, delirium after stress in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism → 911.
Levothyroxine: empty stomach, apart from calcium and iron; half-life 6–10 days; TSH still high = raise the dose; raises warfarin's effect.
Methimazole first; PTU in the first trimester and storm (liver). Both can cause agranulocytosis: fever, sore throat, ulcers.
Radioactive iodine never in pregnancy; amiodarone (iodine) causes hypo or hyper.
Papillary: lymphatics, psammoma bodies. Follicular: invasion, blood. Medullary: C cells, calcitonin, RET, MEN 2. Anaplastic: fast, fatal.
PTH: calcium up, phosphate down, activates 1α-hydroxylase; acts on osteoblasts. Calcitonin: inhibits osteoclasts.
Primary hyperparathyroidism: Ca high, P low, PTH high; adenoma; lost lamina dura, brown tumors. Secondary: kidney failure.
Hypoparathyroidism (after thyroidectomy): Ca low, P high, PTH low; Chvostek and Trousseau. Pseudo: PTH high.
Rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults; the recurrent laryngeal nerve is at risk in thyroid surgery (hoarseness).
he-diabetes: Beta = insulin (about 70%), alpha = glucagon, delta = somatostatin (brakes both).
Glucose → GLUT2 → ATP → K-ATP closes → depolarization → calcium in → insulin. Sulfonylureas close K-ATP.
C-peptide 1:1 with your own insulin: low in type 1 and with injected insulin.
Insulin: GLUT4 in muscle and fat, storage, potassium into cells. Glucagon: liver only, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketones.
Diagnosis: HbA1c 6.5% or more, fasting 126 or more, OGTT 200 or more. Prediabetes 5.7–6.4%. Control: HbA1c below 7%.
Type 1: autoimmune, C-peptide low, DKA. Type 2: resistance, insulin ineffective not deficient.
Metformin first: no lows, GI upset, B12, lactic acidosis, stop below eGFR 30.
Lows and weight gain: insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides. Weight loss: GLP-1 agonists (C-cell warning), SGLT2.
SGLT2: yeast infections, UTIs. TZD: edema, heart failure. DPP-4: mild, oral. Acarbose: treat lows with glucose.
Rapid insulins 5–15 min (meals); glargine basal about 24 h; degludec over 42 h.
Mouth: periodontitis (two-way link), xerostomia, candidiasis, burning mouth, delayed healing.
Low in the chair: awake → 15–20 g sugar by mouth; unconscious → glucagon 1 mg IM, call 911. Morning visits, confirm the meal.
he-repro: FSH → Sertoli (ABP, inhibin, AMH, blood-testis barrier). LH → Leydig (testosterone). Inhibin lowers FSH; testosterone lowers GnRH and LH.
Outside testosterone: T high, LH and FSH low, small testes, low count. Failing testes: T low, LH and FSH high.
Two cells: LH → theca → androgens; FSH → granulosa → aromatase → estradiol.
High sustained estradiol → positive feedback → LH surge → ovulation; luteal phase fixed at 14 days (progesterone).
Estradiol = cycle, estriol = pregnancy, estrone = menopause. Menopause: FSH and LH high.
hCG rescues the corpus luteum (pregnancy test). Placenta: hCG, hPL (anti-insulin), progesterone, estriol, not oxytocin.
Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects it. Suckling: dopamine down, prolactin up; prolactin suppresses GnRH.
Clots: the pill, menopausal estrogen, tamoxifen, raloxifene. Tamoxifen stimulates the uterus (endometrial cancer).
Leuprolide (continuous GnRH) shuts down LH and FSH; finasteride blocks DHT; bicalutamide blocks the receptor; anastrozole blocks aromatase.
Seminoma: commonest, radiosensitive; yolk sac = AFP, choriocarcinoma = hCG; cryptorchidism risk stays after surgery.
BPH: transition zone, obstruction. Prostate cancer: peripheral zone, PSA, osteoblastic metastases, Gleason.
HPV 16/18 → cervical neoplasia at the transformation zone; 6/11 → condyloma. Pregnancy → gingivitis and pyogenic granuloma.
he-heme: White cells, most to least: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils (Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas).
Neutrophil: bacteria first. Eosinophil: parasites, allergy (major basic protein). Basophil: histamine. Monocyte → macrophage.
CD4 helper: MHC II. CD8 cytotoxic: MHC I. NK: kills cells missing MHC I; CD16 binds IgG (ADCC).
Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow (B) and thymus (T) only. PALS = T cells in the spleen's white pulp; paracortex = T cells in the node.
Thymus stroma = epithelioreticular cells; involutes to fat by the teens.
Iron deficiency: microcytic, low ferritin, glossitis, angular cheilitis, Plummer-Vinson. B12: macrocytic, beefy tongue, numbness, pernicious anemia.
Acute leukemia: 20% or more blasts. AML: adults, Auer rods; APL t(15;17), DIC, ATRA. ALL: children, no Auer rods.
CML: t(9;22) BCR-ABL1, every stage of maturation, imatinib. CLL: over 70, small B cells, smudge cells.
Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg, central nodes, contiguous, curable. Non-Hodgkin: mostly B-cell, scattered, extranodal.
Burkitt t(8;14) MYC, starry sky, African jaw, EBV. Follicular t(14;18) BCL2. Mantle t(11;14). MALT: H. pylori, Sjögren.
Myeloma: CRAB, M-spike, punched-out jaw lesions. NK/T: EBV, perforated palate.
Gingival enlargement, petechiae, pallor → CBC with differential and referral; defer elective care with very low neutrophils or platelets.
mg-giphys: Gastrin: G cells (antrum); peptides, stretch, vagus via GRP; shut off by acid through somatostatin
CCK: I cells; fat and protein; gallbladder contracts, Oddi relaxes, pancreatic enzymes, slows emptying
Secretin: S cells; duodenal pH < 4.5; pancreatic and biliary HCO3- through CFTR; also ↑ pepsinogen, ↓ acid
GIP (K cells) and GLP-1 (L cells): incretins released by glucose, amino acids and fat; insulin up; GLP-1 also slows emptying and appetite (semaglutide; tirzepatide hits both receptors)
Motilin every ~90 min fasting drives the MMC; erythromycin is a motilin agonist
Saliva: isotonic in the acinus, hypotonic after the ducts; only nerves control it, and both autonomic divisions stimulate it
Parietal cell: H+/K+ ATPase, intrinsic factor; ACh + gastrin + histamine (histamine potentiates)
Cephalic phase is vagal: vagotomy abolishes it
Enteropeptidase activates trypsin; trypsin activates the rest
Only monosaccharides absorbed: SGLT1 (glucose, galactose), GLUT5 (fructose), GLUT2 out
Fat: micelles in, chylomicrons out to lymph; bile salts recycled in the terminal ileum
Cholera = secretory (cAMP, CFTR); lactose intolerance = osmotic
Pancreatic juice stays isotonic (ducts add HCO3-), under nerves plus secretin and CCK; colipase is secreted as procolipase
Segmentation contracts mid-bolus and mixes; peristalsis contracts behind and relaxes ahead, and propels
GERD: transient LES relaxations, resting tone usually normal; achalasia: VIP/NO neurons lost, the LES can't relax
Short- and medium-chain fatty acids → portal blood; long-chain → chylomicrons → lymph, bypassing the liver; the colon has no villi
Vomiting: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; diarrhea: HCO3- loss, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
Liver makes albumin and clotting factors but not VIII; zone 1 makes urea and glucose; zone 3 does CYP450 and glutamine and dies first (hypoxia, acetaminophen)
Bilirubin: albumin-bound → conjugated with glucuronide in the liver → bile → urobilinogen → stercobilin (stool) and urobilin (urine)
mg-gianat: Celiac = foregut (to the major papilla); SMA = midgut (to 2/3 transverse colon); IMA = hindgut (to the pectinate line)
Pain: foregut epigastric, midgut umbilical (T10), hindgut suprapubic
Appendicitis: periumbilical (visceral) then McBurney point (parietal peritoneum)
Posterior duodenal ulcer bleeds from the gastroduodenal artery
Varices: left gastric-azygos; caput medusae: paraumbilical; rectal: superior-inferior rectal
Below the arcuate line only transversalis fascia lies behind the rectus
MDs don't LIe: medial = direct (Hesselbach), lateral = indirect (deep ring)
IVC T8, esophagus T10, aorta T12
Duodenum Brunner glands; jejunum tallest plicae; ileum Peyer patches/M cells; colon no villi
Chief cells: basophilic, pepsinogen; parietal cells: eosinophilic, HCl + intrinsic factor
Filiform papillae have no taste buds; parotid all serous (largest, about 30% of saliva), submandibular mostly serous (about 60%), sublingual mostly mucous (about 5%)
Zone 3 (central vein): least O2, most CYP450, first hit by ischemia and acetaminophen; Ito cells store vitamin A
Pancreaticoduodenal arteries: the only celiac–SMA link; marginal artery (of Drummond): SMA–IMA; splenic flexure = watershed, first to go ischemic
Portal vein lies in front of the IVC; portal-caval anastomoses carry almost nothing until portal pressure rises
Intussusception: usually ileocolic, 3 months–6 years; diverticula: sigmoid colon, older people
Meissner (submucosal) = secretion and blood flow; Auerbach (myenteric, between the muscle layers) = motility
Plica = mucosa + submucosal core; villus = mucosa only (lamina propria core, lacteal)
Centroacinar cells, no striated ducts, no myoepithelial cells = pancreas; striated ducts = salivary gland
Liver: blood → central vein; bile (canaliculi → canals of Hering → ducts) and lymph (space of Disse) → portal tract
mg-gipath: GERD erodes the palatal surfaces of maxillary teeth; Barrett (goblet cells) leads to adenocarcinoma
Esophageal SCC: alcohol and tobacco; Mallory-Weiss: tear after vomiting
H. pylori: urease and ammonia; top cause of chronic gastritis; about 42% of US ulcers; first line bismuth quadruple (PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline)
NSAID ulcers: lost prostaglandins; misoprostol prevents them (not in pregnancy)
Celiac: anti-tTG IgA, villous atrophy, aphthae, enamel defects, dermatitis herpetiformis
Crohn: mouth to anus, skip, transmural, granulomas, fistulas. UC: rectum up, continuous, mucosal
C. diff after clindamycin: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin; no antimotility drugs
Gardner (APC): jaw osteomas + supernumerary teeth; Peutz-Jeghers: perioral pigment + hamartomas
Hep A/E fecal-oral, acute only (E: up to 25% die in pregnancy); B vaccine; C mostly chronic, no vaccine, curable, linked to oral lichen planus; D needs B
Hemochromatosis = iron (HFE, low TIBC, phlebotomy); Wilson = copper (ATP7B, young, low ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer)
Cirrhosis patient: check INR and platelets; acetaminophen ≤ 2 g/day; avoid NSAIDs

Precision = repeatable; accuracy = true. Standardization = same rules; calibration = scores agree.
Incidence = new cases over time (cohort); prevalence = existing cases now (cross-sectional).

A ratio of 1 = no difference, above 1 = harmful, below 1 = protective; a CI that includes 1 = not significant.
NNT = 1/ARR, rounded up; lower is better.
Type I = false positive (alpha, 0.05); type II = false negative (beta); power = 1 − beta.

rd-physics: Cathode (−) makes electrons; anode (+) tungsten target; >99% heat, ~1% x-rays.
Bremsstrahlung = primary source (continuous spectrum); characteristic = minor.
mA and time = photon quantity; kVp = energy/penetration (beam quality).

Filtration removes low-energy photons; collimation restricts beam, cuts scatter and dose.
